items.body: One has to admire the boldness of the opening of Cacciamali. It doesn’t try to dazzle; instead, it opts for understated playfulness. A faltering folk wind instrument sets the tone as if the player were testing it rather than performing on it. This is not an artist trying to impress but someone searching. Rosso Polare introduces the album as an act of exploration. The hesitant breaths soon give way to rougher growls before the music gathers momentum through the increasingly insistent drumming of Cinna Peyghamy’s tombak. “Falò” immediately shifts the atmosphere. Beginning with recordings from a bonfire, the track slowly thickens until a guitar emerges from the electroacoustic fabric, introducing one of the album’s rare melodic moments. Its simple folk-like phrase briefly offers a point of orientation before gradually dissolving back into the surrounding texture. Equally striking are the barely audible voices: “la carezza di un ricordo… il rifiuto di un ventre… il rifiuto di una madre… il rifiuto di un figlio…” (“the caress of a memory… the rejection of a womb… the rejection of a mother… the rejection of a son…”). There is no explanation and no obvious narrative. The words are uttered almost like a spell. That reluctance to foreground melody becomes one of the album’s defining characteristics. Even when recognisable instrumental gestures appear, they are never allowed to establish themselves as fixed themes. They emerge briefly before being reabsorbed into a constantly shifting ensemble in which electronics, acoustic instruments and environmental recordings occupy the same musical plane. The collaborations expand this vocabulary without disrupting its coherence. Riccardo Sinigaglia’s presence introduces a subtle dialogue between electronic abstraction and ritual memory. “Monte” overlays dense electronic textures with ritualistic drumming, children’s voices and the distant bells of grazing animals, creating a landscape that feels inhabited rather than merely observed. “Hastilude” — named after the medieval martial games derived from hasta (spear) and ludus (play) — is one of the album’s thickest sonic environments, its layers continually reshaping one another without ever settling into stable hierarchies. “1744”, created with HMOT (Stas Shärifulla), opens in an almost cinematic manner, or perhaps like the score to a contemporary dance piece, before gradually giving way to the denser electronic textures that characterise the album’s second half. The liner notes provide an illuminating framework without dictating how the music should be heard. Side A draws upon the rhythmic traditions of medieval quintain games and flag throwing, while Side B is structured around a local legend recounting a fatal duel between father and son in 1744. Yet Rosso Polare avoids illustrating either narrative. Instead, ritual and rupture become compositional principles: repetition gradually gives way to fracture, while tradition quietly coexists with loss. Equally important is the album’s treatment of place and everyday life. No location is identified, yet the accents of the spoken voices suggest northern Italy, while one overheard remark hints that the recordings were made shortly before Christmas. These details are never highlighted; they simply exist alongside the music. In “La Cruma”, snippets of perfectly intelligible conversation drift in and out of the texture without carrying any obvious symbolic meaning. They are not clues to be deciphered but reminders that this music belongs to inhabited places. Throughout the album, field recordings never function as scenic decoration. They remain part of the same sonic fabric as the instruments and electronics. That approach has characterised Rosso Polare’s work from the beginning. Whether in Lettere Animali, Bocca d’Ombra or Campo Amaro — whose “Testamento Fermo” includes an impromptu chorus formed by those present — his music has consistently embraced participation over authorship. Cacciamali is the first album released after the departure of Anna Vezzosi, yet it continues this collective ethos. Collaboration is never ornamental; it is embedded in the way the music is conceived. The title itself, Cacciamali (“chasing away evils”), inevitably recalls Ernesto de Martino’s studies of ritual and popular belief in southern Italy, particularly La terra del rimorso, alongside Diego Carpitella’s groundbreaking field recordings documenting music as a means of confronting suffering and uncertainty. Rosso Polare never quotes those traditions directly, but he seems to share an ethnomusicologist’s curiosity. His music occupies a space where free improvisation, folk memory and traces of pagan ritual coexist without hierarchy. Whistling, traditional flutes, environmental sound, electronics and percussion are granted equal importance, while the natural world and human presence continually overlap. Rather than reconstructing folklore, Cacciamali uncovers the fragile traces it leaves behind, allowing stories, landscapes and communities to emerge through listening rather than explanation. To paraphrase Alice in Wonderland, “What is the use of music with no pictures or conversations?” Cacciamali has both in sonic form. Rosso Polare photo courtesy the artist To find out more on how to chase away evils, I reached out to Rosso Polare for an interview conducted by email, after which I followed up with a couple of clarifications. One of the things I found most compelling about Cacciamali is that it never separates music from the world around it. Environmental recordings, recognisable human voices and fragments of everyday conversations continually drift in and out of the texture. They never function as documentary material, but neither do they become anonymous sound objects. Instead, they anchor the music within a living environment. How do you approach the relationship between field recordings and instrumental sound? At what point does an environmental recording stop being documentation and become part of the composition? Since the beginning of Rosso Polare, the threshold between environmental recording and tonal sound has always been some sort of challenge. In the project’s body of work, field recordings are simply treated as integral sonic material within the composition, and it’s more a matter of a mental shift: giving the same relevance to material that could generally be seen as background, and striving to put it on the same level as composed sound. On the other hand, it’s also about stepping down with regard to played music: treating it, as much as possible, as if it were a “piece of the story” rather than the highlight of the specific musician who played it. This very difficult proposition is an attempt to make these two distinct habitats coexist without one being preponderant over the other. When does an environmental recording stop being documentation? I guess it happens in a very gradual way for me, as I gather sounds with no particular structure in mind in the first place and then assemble them afterward in the studio. Though I usually tend to avoid modern human anthropophony, it’s only with the last two albums, Campo Amaro and Cacciamali, that Rosso Polare started to embrace a bit of that as well. Before that, the project leaned away from the human voice in order to make the pieces feel as “in and out of this world” as possible, I would say. On these two albums, on the other hand, there’s some sort of investigation into folklore inside me that still has something to say, I think. So yes, as I gather sounds, they start to become part of a bigger picture, but they are always treated as just sounds, in much the same way that I treat instruments. I recently spoke to Cinna Peyghamy, who described improvisation as “moderating a debate between two very different speakers.” Listening to “XIV – Pavo”, that image immediately came to mind. He brings multiphonics and an extraordinary physicality to the opening track, yet they seem to become part of a much larger sonic organism rather than taking centre stage. What attracted you to Cinna’s approach to sound, and how did the dialogue between the two of you shape the identity of the piece? I met Cinna a while back in Basel. At the time, Rosso Polare was still a duo and we were playing at Würm on the very same night as him. Stas Shärifulla, a very good friend and artist I greatly admire, had invited both acts to play, and we almost instantly connected. I really like Cinna’s quote here and find it very fitting in this conversation too. “xiv – pavo” is the opening piece of what is, for me, a very difficult album, an album about balancing both music and personal emotions, making peace with changing aspects of my life. Thematically, it started with the concept of quintain games, flag throwing specifically, as the main melodic column is made of environmental recordings from a flag-throwing game in Spoleto, which, uncommonly these days, featured horns alongside the classic drumming. Once back in the studio, I mangled these recordings into rhythmic patterns, and the horns that came with them got weird in a very interesting way: rather than resembling a specific melody, they became some sort of average fantasy of Italian folk music, not as a cliché but more out of a damaged memory, I’d say. Alongside that came what I’d describe as embracing my limitations: between starting and finishing the recording, I contracted a severe form of pneumonia, which highly affected my lung capacity and, subsequently, my ability to play wind instruments for long periods. Lots of whispers, pants, breath struggles and inhaled screams were sampled and implemented as assets to the track rather than obstacles in the process. Cinna’s drumming and modular processing added great counterpoint to the already complex patterns of the track, while also grounding the second part of the piece in a more upfront dimension of musicality. His command of the tombak is really beyond anyone I’ve had the chance to listen to, and the integration of this very tactile instrument with modular synthesis is as difficult as it gets. I felt this track was a fitting opportunity to collaborate. He received from me what was, at the time, a somewhat finished part, and the dialogue started from that. You know, how do you integrate your voice into this? What and when should you play? Stylistic questions more than technicalities, I think, ideas about the shape of the music. The role of this track as an opener was really hard to frame in the first place. The one before was an album about Italian folk traditional chants and their potential for a modern adaptation, and I still thought that thread had to be developed in some way, so that’s when the quintain came in. But, in parallel, I came across a local legend about a son dueling with his father and being fatally struck in 1744 in Lombardy, which sort of acted as a hidden subtext throughout the record, picking up this sense of loss and despair I felt while finishing the album. So “xiv – pavo“ is basically an introduction to a specific habitat for me. One aspect I found particularly interesting is that Cacciamali brings together musicians who already share artistic connections. For instance, as a curator of the Korkut Triennale, Stas Shärifulla (HMOT) invited Cinna Peyghamy to perform while Riccardo Sinigaglia comes from an entirely different generation of Italian electronic music. Rather than sounding like a collection of guest appearances, the album feels like the meeting point of several different experimental music communities. Was that network of relationships something you consciously wanted to bring together, and did those existing connections influence the way the collaborations developed? Firstly, all appearances on the record are either friends or musicians I met and shared a vision with. Stas, with his wife Julia, was part of the label (Klammklang, now inactive) that published Rosso Polare’s first album, Lettere Animali, in 2020. We’ve been friends ever since, and I was really happy to finally collaborate on something in the studio. Cinna Peyghamy, as said before, has been a staple connection since the show in Basel and resonated both in ideas and music. Riccardo Sinigaglia is the unsung hero of experimental underground music in Italy since the ’80s. I fell in love with the debut of his band, Futuro Antico, a stunning example of cosmic experimentation that went beyond Italian music at the time. We met back in 2021 at Bääfest in Milano and connected. For me, his appearance on the record is a way to continue something that happened closer to me, a sort of homage to my musical ancestry, in a way. The beauty of this scene is the possibility of bringing together communities, as you suggested: having friends representing different scenes of experimental music and making the ends meet altogether, be it on recorded media or live performances. This network is something you build along the way through true bonds and experiences. In Cacciamali, the aim was to bring together, on record, this friendship and kin built along the way. Throughout the album I had the impression that you compose less by arranging sounds than by allowing them to find relationships with one another. Even the improvised pieces display an extraordinary sense of formal control, while the more structured works never lose their spontaneity. I’m curious about your working process. When you’re developing a piece, what tells you that it has reached its final form? Is it a question of balance, density, resonance, or is there another criterion you rely on before deciding that nothing more needs to be added—or taken away? My process relies heavily on spontaneity, followed by very meticulous arranging which, as you rightly pointed out, strives to find relationships and conversation between them. I like to think of my pieces as chapters of a book or acts in a movie. Even though it’s usually not that pondered in the recording stage, I start with a few ideas. Lately, it’s more about a series of “what ifs”: “What if this melody idea goes on top of this field recording?” or “What if I record this sound in this way?” or “What if I prepare a guitar with these objects?” etc. I don’t really like to know the themes of my works at the start. At the same time, I know when I’m working on a series of tracks that will be part of a whole, and I like to think that the themes and concepts I later find words for were actually inside the sounds all along. So it’s more like extracting what I’m trying to say from the music itself. I’d say lately it’s become more common for me to have a few stories or loose thoughts in mind at the start. Then there’s a very long time that I spend rearranging and mixing, continuously questioning myself, the tracks and sounds inside, but in a properly healthy way. I’m very picky, to the point that I even annoy myself at times, so it’s a bit of a struggle. Part of me wants to get the most out of the record, but I still need to fight this race for perfection, as it’s easy to lose a fair bit of spontaneity in the music. I always want it to feel slightly rough and to retain a sense of momentum as well. When a piece has reached its final form? Fearing here that I might sound a bit trivial, but for me it’s also a matter of gut feeling. My role is to serve the music, much as a messenger serves his purpose, and I try to sense when my part is done. Usually, a piece is ready when it feels like it’s become part of the story as a whole, when it’s telling its part of the album and feels worthy of its conversation. As a follow up, since you mentioned you had pneumonia, so did you play the flute one can hear at the very beginning of the album while recovering? The flute playing at the beginning is the only flute I don’t play. I recorded it in Switzerland at the Goetheanum. On a hill, there was a man playing a sort of Buffalo Horn. I was with Stas, curiously enough. All the other flutes on the album, however, are mostly bamboo, very rough-hewn, both transverse and with traditional mouthpieces. I think there’s also a metal transverse flute at times, and a couple of recorders, of two different sizes (soprano and tenor, I think). From the pneumonia period, the wind instruments featured are mainly the simplest to play, the small ones that require less air, plus, of course, the various reworked rattles you hear. Finally, could you confirm that the voices one can hear in the track “la cruma” were recorded in Lombardy in northern Italy? Exactly, the “Cruma” recordings come from the province of Lombardy. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: Rosso Polare 的《Cacciamali》以探索而非炫技的姿态展开。开场以一支试探性的民间管乐器引入，随即汇入打击乐手 Cinna Peyghamy 的 tombak 鼓声，文本逐渐转为粗粝的低吼。专辑融合电子声学织体、原声乐器与环境录音，旋律片段短暂浮现后便消融回不断变形的音层之中。歌词以近乎咒语的低声念诵呈现，缺乏叙事逻辑，成为声音素材的一部分。合作者 Riccardo Sinigaglia 带来电子抽象与仪式记忆的微妙对话，HMOT 参与的作品则呈现近乎电影配乐的开篇气质。专辑结构借鉴中世纪枪术竞技与抛旗仪式，另一面围绕 1744 年父子决斗的当地传说，但音乐拒绝直接图解文本，仪式与断裂本身成为作曲方法。

items.body: Chicago-based drummer and composer Gustavo Coritñas is a restless experimenter. His music often includes Latin American folk influences, sociopolitical awareness, and thrilling spontaneity. On The Drum Also Sings, Cortiñas joins forces with two other unique and stylistically very different drummers, Dave King and Isaiah Spencer, to explore the drum kit's lyricism. For instance, the three-part group improvisation, “Dialogue with the Ancestors” features a definite spirituality. Its chant-like refrains and fiery yet haunting rhythms build an exalted homage to the gods of the past and the primal world itself. Here too, the contrasting styles of the three drummers add another captivating dimension to the piece. King’s exuberant percussion with touches of whimsy, heard on the right, complements Spencer’s darkly hued thundering beats on the left. While Cortiñas, in between his bandmates, adds a contemplative, almost meditative aspect to the collective drumming. Despite the individuality of each musician, the result is delightfully cohesive, stimulating yet never jarring. The theme of transcendent mysticism runs through the entire album. On “Etinel skotol t'ixt'unel” Mayan spoken word artist Angelina Suyul recites her own poem in her ancestral tongue. A paen to the eternal and the integration of humanity within the universe, Suyul’s performance moves with the hypnotic cadence of her words. Their meaning is almost instinctively understood even before reading the Spanish and English translations. Chilean vocalist La Paula Herrera delivers Cortiñas’ song “Tu Resiliencia Es Resistencia” with emotional resonance. Her sublime artistry and eloquence amplify the hopefulness and the poignancy of the lyrics. Meanwhile, the intimacy of her voice and the fluidity of her singing enchant and mesmerize. On “Añay Pachamama” Argentinian musician Maryta de Humahuaca interprets her compatriot, María Farfán Caparros’ ode in the Quechua language. The track glorifies the natural world in a pantheistic tone. The title translates to “Gratitude Mother Earth”, and de Humahuaca imbues it with an appropriate balance of the sacred and the primal. It is simultaneously a joyous and somber religious ceremony. This conceptual framework continues with vocalist and clarinetist Anget Bat Dawid, who transforms “Psalm 23” into a powerful, impassioned plea. Her thrillingly dissonant clarinet and her bluesy shouts make this biblical verse into a life-affirming protest anthem. It also serves as the perfect conclusion for this intriguing and provocative work. On the surface, a recording made up primarily of drumming, with little other instrumentation, may sound daunting. Coritñas, however, has made it evocative enough to entrance his audience. Far from mainstream, The Drum Also Sings stirs open-minded listeners to their core. The Drum Also Sings by Gustavo Cortiñas Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / improvisation / world fusion / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以鼓为主要载体，由三位风格迥异的鼓手协作，探索打击乐器的歌唱性与抒情表达。三部分集体即兴作品《Dialogue with the Ancestors》在圣歌式节奏中构建灵性对话，不同鼓手的音色与律动形成互补，兼具仪式感与自发性。专辑穿插玛雅语诗歌朗诵、智利声乐、盖丘亚语赞美诗，以及将《诗篇23》转化为生命抗争呼号的改编曲，使拉丁美洲原住民文化、部落记忆与自由即兴、实验声响相结合。尽管以鼓为主，但通过人声和节奏层次变化，保持了叙事张力与精神维度，呈现超越性神秘主义主题。

items.body: Vertical London does exactly what it says on the can, establishing its premise from the very first minutes through a recording of birds and planes over Loughborough Junction. It is a sound I immediately recognised after spending twenty years living beneath the same flight path in South London, but Kate Carr approaches this familiar collision without lamenting noise pollution or searching nostalgically for a disappearing city. Birds and aircraft occupy the same acoustic plane, each accepted as part of London’s everyday ecology. From there, Carr moves through Tube stations buried beneath the city, the Greenwich Foot Tunnel, shopping centres, parks and lifts inside the Shard, eventually looking back down at London stretching and twinkling below. Verticality becomes a way of listening to the city across its different levels. Although the record follows a journey across the capital, it never feels like a collection of sonic postcards. London identifies itself only in passing, through station announcements, tannoys mentioning the River Thames or fragments of public transport. People are everywhere, yet they seldom become protagonists. Conversations remain indistinct, with voices often arriving through loudspeakers instead of direct encounters. Titles such as “I don’t think you can hear but people largely discussed dogs all the way back to central London” quietly acknowledge the limitations of field recording itself: microphones never quite capture the same experience as the person carrying them. One of the album’s greatest pleasures lies in its humour. Carr’s wonderfully verbose titles continually reshape the act of listening. “Celebrating a squeaky transport barrier…”, “A very long queue for the London Eye which is quite shit…”, or “It was New Year’s Day after all, and yes someone really was playing this at the overground station” all display a dry self-deprecation that gently punctures any temptation towards field-recording solemnity. The joke is never directed at the sounds themselves, but at the expectations we bring to them. The album takes listening seriously without ever taking itself too seriously. A loose temporal framework also runs through the work. New Year’s Day appears only through fleeting details: someone wishing “Happy New Year” in Bloomsbury, an unexpected instrumental rendition of “Auld Lang Syne” at an Overground station. There are no celebrations or drunken crowds. The city simply carries on, making the choice of date feel quietly counterintuitive. Carr documents a public holiday through a London seemingly suspended between one year and the next. The only explicit intellectual companion appears during the visit to Kilburn. At one point Carr quietly records herself (assuming it is her voice) saying the neighbourhood’s name, almost as if she were leaving a spoken geotag for reference. It has the feel of an aide-mémoire accidentally left in the finished work, but it also introduces Doreen Massey into the album. From this point, ideas about place begin to inform the act of listening itself. Massey’s understanding of place as something continually produced through movement, memory and social relations quietly echoes throughout the record. Every location remains connected to the next. High-frequency tones drift between recordings, drones appear among the crows and dinosaurs of Crystal Palace, and even Hampstead is characterised by the whisper imposed by private security and the sense of controlled space. London emerges as a continuum, its locations connected through sound and movement. What I admire most about Vertical London is its trust in ordinary experience. Carr never appears to chase spectacular recordings. The only “climax” arrives midway through with a couple of “high drama” moments which are anything but. Both “Dramatic build-up to when I dipped into the shopping centre to find a man playing piano outside Aldi” and “Dramatic drummers on the street as I ran due to being late for my Shard viewing platform booking” animate the narrative with suitably understated theatricality. Carr allows the city to reveal itself through patient walking, public transport, chance encounters and small acts of attention. A squeaking ticket barrier, electromagnetic harmonics from the DLR and birds beneath aircraft all receive the same careful consideration. By the end of the journey, landmarks have receded into a living acoustic fabric, where every layer—from the tunnels beneath the streets to the flight paths overhead—contributes to the city’s constantly shifting identity. To walks us through the album, we have asked Kate Carr to answer a few questions for us by email. You are a dedicated walker. One of your recent sonic explorations has been Transect – Heathrow perimeter walk with bird horns. You have circled London and frequently go on walks when traveling whether that might be in Italy or China. For this album, which is not strictly speaking just a walk as public transport is an integral part of it, you’re constantly moving between birds and planes over Loughborough Junction, the deep Tube stations, the Greenwich Foot Tunnel beneath the Thames, lift shafts inside the Shard, and eventually looking out over the city from above. What made you decide verticality was going to become the organising idea this time round? Has living under the flight pathway in a city with an extensive underground system made you more conscious of what’s above and what’s below, so to speak? And did you have any expectations of the sounds, frequencies, resonances you were going to find? I think ever since I did my album Midsummer, London a few years back and went across the city from one side to another on that long summer solstice day, I was sort of mulling what other sorts of trajectories I could trace. I was thinking about this vertical one for a while as it is obviously on the face of it a very different journey to moving across the city, and I suppose I wondered just how different it would actually be, both the experience of undertaking it and also how different it might sound within the recordings themselves. Movement and journeys are really central to my work, I am always asking: what version of this route is my movement producing in a recording, this combination of the chance elements, how I am recording, what gear I am using, my own personhood and identity and what or who I encounter. For a long while now I am interested in recording as a trace of how all those things come together, and what aural fragments of these encounters and moments is recorded or indeed not recorded by the in the recording device. In terms of time spent at different verticalities, I have spent a lot of time obviously on the tube as most commuters have, but comparatively very little in London’s higher reaches. In doing the album I was interested in if elevation could be heard somehow or other, can something sound higher up? Or lower down? And I was also interested in the zigzag journey I was undertaking to bring me to these various elevations in the city. So it was a few different layers or questions to the project. I think yes you are probably very right that living under the the flight path has influenced my thinking about the vertical, I was actually planning at one point that the highest point in the album might be a recording from inside a plane, but once I decided to do it on New Year’s Day this was shelved as an idea. The final component to the album as I was thinking about it revolved around the darkness of winter in London, I liked the idea of getting higher and higher, and closer to the sun as a way of gesturing towards the difficulties of this long dark period, and then this idea of the new year, new me sort of thing, and how the experience of new year’s day itself sort of punctures this. In the jumble of all these things the project lurks. Human presence is felt, as it is to be expected since this is an urban work, but it is not always discernible, the only distinct speech one can hear come from “institutional” sources, loudspeakers, recorded voices, or formulaic propositions. Is this because of ethical concerns or purely for compositional purposes? There are some voices in it, just snippets of people passing me, one person wishing another happy new year, and the sorts of murmurs you hear when moving through locations. I did not deliberately leave out conversations in this work, but I do have ethical considerations in regard to this issue. My practice is centred on the traces of activities, encounters, moments which unfold in public space, both ones I can be heard in and ones I am not. I think there is something of value in recording in public space in this sort of fragmentary and incomplete way, but that said there are of course conversations and encounters which I would choose not to use and would not consider it ok for me to use. In this case it was a cold, dark and quiet day, I was moving fairly quickly through locations and what reached me were just these small fragments. The work is meant to convey the experience of commuting and I guess purposeful movement rather than the drift of psychogeography. Of course as we move through public space we do sometimes get drawn into listening to other people’s conversations, but here the work is more about an experience of being in my own head and thoughts, while also encountering these fragments of other people also going about their days. One thing that really struck me is just how funny Vertical London is. Not because anything overtly comic happens, but because your titles quietly reframe what we’re about to hear. “Celebrating a squeaky transport barrier”, “A very long queue for the London Eye which is quite shit…”, “Dramatic build-up to when I dipped into the shopping centre to find a man playing piano outside Aldi…”—they all have this wonderfully dry, self-deprecating humour that somehow makes you listen more carefully rather than less. Field recording and sound art can sometimes take themselves rather seriously, yet Vertical London never does. It seems to embrace chance, anticlimax and the absurdity of everyday urban life without diminishing the act of listening itself. Do the titles emerge naturally from the walks, or have they become your way of gently keeping both the practice of field recording—and yourself—in check? Ha, well I am glad you found it funny. I do find humour just a really important component of basically just life. Not in a distancing way, or even in a not taking things seriously way but more just than humour and delight are part of the fabric of existence. I basically very often am quite astonished by people and what they do and say, and how different we all are from the smallest to the biggest things, and taking a trip and how this unfolds is no different. I find what people do, how they are in public space, how we encounter each other and organise ourselves sometimes just really charming, of course other times quite sad or even surreal. I think undertaking this very random project on New Year’s Day just sort of adds to that feeling. Here I am racing to these different parts of London for no real reason except to see what they sound like and what is happening in them, encountering all sorts of people doing their own things, and in all of that there are just really absurd and bizarrely anticlimatic moments, as well moment of rushing and drama. I don’t really feel I need to keep myself in check, or that sound art is too serious or takes itself too seriously, I just think humour is part of my orientation towards the world and others. I title the works after finishing the piece, but they come easily to me really. They just emerge from my memories of the day, both the felt memories and the narrative ones. I really like and enjoy the relationship between words and the sound work itself. I have always enjoyed that aspect of making work. I am basically obsessed with words, so I love to feel the dynamic between the composition itself and the words which accompany it and what this relation generates in terms of an experience of the work. What made you decide to set this work within a 24-hour timeframe, choosing New Year’s day as its anchoring point especially when Vertical London doesn’t feel particularly jubilant or hangover? I was going to possibly do it on the winter solstice so it matched my summer solstice work, and that would have been good as well, but I missed this date as I was busy I think and so I decided on New Year’s Day as I felt this trajectory of moving upwards resonated in quite interesting ways with ideas of new year’s resolutions, new starts, renewal. I did like the dry humour or irony which emerged in undertaking the work where this movement upwards was revealed as a shift into increasingly sterile, managed and privatised spaces. Increasing altitude does not prove revelatory or even particularly uplifting in this work. In terms of the day long time frame, I tend to work with these strict limitations nowadays because I like how the paucity of time infuses the work. It makes it difficult to position the work as an attempt at some sort of ‘portrait’ of London in a definitive way. The strictness of the protocol for me lends the work these connotations of the fragmentary, the gesture, the moment, the random, the arbitrary. In my work I am always seeking to emphasise: here is my journey, full of moments, charm, annoyances, yes absurdities and surreal slices of existence but it is not London itself, just one version of London authored in time, movement and space. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: Kate Carr的《Vertical London》以城市垂直空间为听觉路径，记录伦敦不同高度的环境声，从鸟鸣与飞机共存的空中声景，到地铁、隧道、购物中心、公园乃至碎片大厦电梯内的声响。专辑并不抱怨噪音或怀旧，而是将飞机与鸟鸣视为城市日常生态的一部分，通过车站广播、公共系统提示音和模糊的对话呈现人的存在，却鲜少让具体人物成为主角。幽默的长标题和新年当天的细节（如Bloomsbury的祝福、火车站意外响起的《友谊地久天长》）赋予作品轻盈与反思，同时暗示了实地录音媒介自身的局限——麦克风无法完全复现亲历者的体验。整张专辑以垂直维度重组城市聆听，既严肃对待声音，又不故作庄严。

items.body:
Page One

a column by
Bill Shoemaker

Jin Hi Kim: Living Tones


Jim Hi Kim © 2026 Livia Sa




Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes.  It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy.  It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张九碟合辑回顾了韩国传统乐器玄琴演奏家兼作曲家金熙四十年来的创作与即兴录音生涯。文章聚焦于她在2026年Neuma厂牌发行的《The Jin Hi Kim Collection》精选集，梳理了她如何从韩国传统音乐精英训练中走出，转向电子音乐与作曲，师从Lou Harrison与Terry Riley，并与Kronos Quartet、Derek Bailey等当代音乐大师合作。合辑的核心线索是她对玄琴这一古老乐器的彻底改造——通过计算机接口与信号处理技术，将这种音色相对有限的五尺长传统鲁特琴的声域极大扩展。评论详细描述了她重听早期作品时的惊喜与感慨，特别是那些用西方乐器转译韩国音乐、运用图形谱法的实验性创作。五碟用于管弦乐与室内乐作品，四碟记录与Gerry Hemingway、Bill Frisell等打击乐与弦乐演奏家的即兴合作，展现了她在传统根基之上开拓新音乐的完整历程。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz与Francesco Paolo Paladino、Luca Chino Ferrari合作的《Songs of Compassion》，延续了她六十年代实验精神，以非线性的钢琴声响、弦乐与木管交织，构建出反常规和声叙事的音乐场景。歌词兼具诗意与当代政治性，触及威权、种族与死亡，延续了六十年代抗议传统的直接表达。Moskowitz的声音带着疲惫与智慧，像方法派演员般潜入哲学命题；钢琴则如歌队般介入并评论。整体作品既有先锋派的疏离感，又蕴含深切的人文关怀，适合偏爱实验声景与文本深度的听者。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._genre: experimental / global fusion / klezmer / afrobeat / cumbia
items._cn_summary: 该专辑以自制乐器为核心，用废弃物打造的器乐呈现出精准音高与丰富音色，在录音中展现出高质量的声音质感。音乐上融合克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍、桑巴以及中东音阶，旋律与节奏横跨多文化传统，同时加入大量即兴演奏段落，体现演奏者的技术功底。乐评指出，乐队将自制乐器与对应文化风格有效匹配，使每首曲目都带有鲜明的地域色彩，如单簧管演绎犹太民谣、长笛带领拉丁节奏、马林巴配合非洲打击乐等。整张专辑在实验性与可听性之间取得平衡，既延续了首张专辑的混合风格，又进一步探索了声音材料的可能性，并借由垃圾造乐的行为提醒听众：音乐创造不依赖昂贵器材，而源于人对节奏与旋律的本能追求。

items.album: David Dzubinski's "Two Views of a Prayer"
items.artist: Prism Quartet with Tyshawn Sorey, Ursula Rucker, and Carlos Santiago
items.excerpt:

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在2021年疫情期间，于意大利Fazioli钢琴厅进行了一场两小时的无脚本独奏即兴，成为专辑《Sendas》的素材。后期混音中加入了他四十年职业生涯收集的人声片段、打击乐、循环、田野录音和环境声效。作品遵循Monk式“绝不重复演奏同一遍”的理念，在沉思与自发创造之间展开，融合了古巴传统、爵士即兴与前卫声响实验。Sosa刻意回避风格标签，强调“少即是多”，以第一遍弹奏为灵魂的自然之声，并在专辑中嵌入关于精神进化与传统的思考。专辑在保留钢琴原声质感的同时，通过稀疏的电子化处理拓展了声音维度，适合关注即兴、实验声响与跨文化融合的听众。

items.body: To accompany his article on Aspen Edities in The Wire 512, Peter Margasak compiles an annotated playlist of tracks from the Belgium label There’s nothing unusual about the fact that Belgian guitarist Ruben Machtelinckx started a label to release his own music. But as his Aspen Edities imprint approaches its tenth anniversary next year, the scope of the project has steadily, if quietly, expanded and changed. The label’s carefully curated catalogue has chronicled that development release by release, with almost every subsequent title carving out fresh terrain while simultaneously honouring its meditative but exploratory roots. The following playlist explores Aspen Edities’ subtly shifting outlook. Christian Wallumrød Ensemble “New hum old hum” From Non Sonett (2026) Pointing to the ECM roots of the Christian Wallumrød Ensemble is too simple. While Aspen Edities label runner Machtelinckx loves the label, the singular collision of indelible, old fashioned chamber melodies and harmonically focused expanses of sustained sound in the pianist/composer’s music feels like the stronger connection. Wallumrød continues an instinctual engagement with electronics, offering a built-on contrast when placed next to the rustic church music feel, and, as heard on the adroitly titled “New hum old hum”, explores tiptoeing gauzy timbral clouds fed through the prism of alternate tunings. Machtelinckx/Badenhorst/Cools/Gouband“Structure 6” From Porous Structures (2019) In some way the arc of the Aspen Edities’ aesthetic can be traced through Machtelinckx’s own work. This richly atmospheric quartet recording features his guitar playing clinging to vestiges of his jazz roots, with shades of Ralph Towner emanating from his interplay with fellow guitarist Bert Cools (Merope). The sui generis sound world of French drummer Tomas Gouband, who prefers to employ tree branches and stones rather than brushes and sticks on his kit, carves out a thick resonance, amplified by generous reverb, while the great Belgian artist Joachim Badenhorst toggles between liquid clarinet melodies and wordless vocals, à la Arve Henriksen. Graden/Agnas/Landin/Bromander “Chimär” From Words Were Coming Out Of Our Ears (2025) The label tapped into the Swedish scene earlier this year with this superb quartet, in which bassists Pär Ola Landen and Vilhelm Bromander actively swap and double up on roles, adding melody and fracturing time within a sub-internal dialogue. The drowsy tempos, laid out with exquisite elasticity by drummer Nils Agnas, and harmonically draped by the feather stroke touch of pianist Johan Graden, loosely evoke the legacy of fellow Scandinavian drummer Jon Christensen and pianist Bobo Stenson, but they inject a more contemporary elegant concision and directness. Dans Les Arbres “les yeux écoutent” From L’Album Vert (2024) The French-Norwegian quartet Dans Les Arbes have carved out a beguiling world of sustained tones and elusive textures on its recordings for ECM, Hubro and Sofa, but they found a simpatico landing spot for L’Album Vert, which maintains a meticulous rigour and attention to detail while embracing the fresh presence of electronic gestures and irregular rhythmic disruptions. Percussionist Ingar Zach, pedal steel guitarist Ivar Grydeland, clarinetist Xavier Charles and keyboardist Christian Wallumrød all possess extended timbral vocabularies, but they function as a single organism. Linus & BPB “Little Jesus, Mighty God” From The Outside, The Music Of Jules De Corte (2026) This new album reinforces the label’s unpredictability and breadth, as Machtelinckx’s longtime project with reedist Thomas Jillings takes a left turn into pop territory. Joined by frequent collaborator Fredrik Leroux and bassist Laurens Smet, the group interprets a selection of tunes by the once popular but now overlooked Jules de Corte, the blind Dutch singer-songwriter and pianist. Jillings translated the lyrics into English and the delicate guitar-centric arrangements make a perfect fit for the gorgeous singing of Bonnie 'Prince' Billy, who helps transform the repertoire, giving it a timeless warmth. Poor Isa “Ply” From Poor Isa + Evan Parker/Ingar Zach (2025) Machtelinckx and frequent cohort Fredrik Leroux started Poor Isa to experiment with some very unusual instrumentation: banjos and woodblocks. Through various extended techniques and the use of e-bows the project has developed a surprisingly broad soundworld, as if some bluegrass pickers were trading fours with a gagaku ensemble. A collaboration with the veteran British saxophonist Evan Parker seemed just as odd, but with the help of regular collaborator, Norwegian percussionist and sound artist Zach, they reveal a shape-shifting versatility. Oker “Crepuscular Rays” From Aerial (2026) This sublime Norwegian group entered the Aspen Edities fold through its Berlin based guitarist Fredrik Rasten, who collaborated with Machtelinckx on his hypnotising solo album Strands Of Lunar Light, a collection of serene experiments in just intonation. Oker got its start composing delicate, folk inspired compositions heavily informed by the improvisational backgrounds of percussionist Jan-Martin Gismervik, bassist Adrian Fiskum Myhr and trumpeter Torstein Lavik Larsen, but over time an attraction to spontaneity has led them to construct their pieces in real time, which Aerial captures. Still, the ensemble builds these delicate, detail-rich extended excursions with structure in mind. Veder“Sedum” From Evergreen (2017) Released in 2017, this is one of the earliest Aspen Edities titles, offering a sonic blueprint that can be connected to many of its recent releases. Machtelinckx’s calmly unfolding guitar and banjo serves as a perfect foil for the unusual braid of horns provided by Norwegian trumpeter Eivind Lønning, Belgian reedist Joachim Badenhorst, and Belgian euphonium player Niels Van Heertum, who composed these stately themes. The music is gentle but introspective, transmitting an unusual strain of chamber jazz that erases any division between extended techniques, contrapuntal elegance, and melodic generosity. Read Peter Margasak’s full Unlimited Editions column on Aspen Edities in The Wire 512. Wire subscribers can also read the article online via the digital magazine library.

items.body: Hardtack is a project founded by Frenchman Alexis Clementides. He is passionate about both technology and music, a recurring theme throughout his education and artistic career. His EP “Radiations” was released in 1999, and now, 27 years later, we have “La Dualité Originelle”, an eight-track album released via Prodam Records. Clementides immersed himself in Electro-Acoustic music, an element that is clearly audible in some of the tracks. However, there is much more to it, with the primary influence lying in what I would simply call Power-Noise. Yet the distinctive—and, to me, fascinating—aspect of his work is the fusion of Power-Noise elements with strings and other sounds that seem to emanate from the background. This gives the music a more accessible quality, creating a blend of Power-Noise and Cinematic soundscapes. It is a varied opus, featuring quieter, almost dreamlike yet abstract passages that suddenly give way to harsher, more brutal sonic onslaughts. “La Dualité Originelle” is an album that pushes boundaries and brings together diverse influences to achieve a creative and intelligent result. (Rating:8). Listen to “L’Ecole De Guerre De La Vie”: L’école de guerre de la vie by HARDTACK About Hardtack Hardtack is the project of French artist Alexis Clementides. His debut EP, “Radiations”, was released in 1999; “La Dualité Originelle” follows twenty-seven years later as his first full-length, issued on Prodam Records (Discogs). Clementides also appears on the 2020 vinyl single “Accident / Yayo88” (Deontologie) as producer. No prior Side-Line coverage of Hardtack has been found.

items.body: Went out three nights in a row Didn’t know what was About to unfold Subject Sue began as an alter ego, but the separation between performer and person has apparently thinned, and you can hear that collapse in the way these songs handle intimacy. Desire becomes partly theatrical, partly confessional, and sometimes faintly ridiculous, which is exactly right. Clubs have always encouraged people to invent themselves for a few hours, then sent them home with makeup fading in the taxi mirror and a head full of decisions that seemed better under red light. Nightlife, in turn, is a place where fantasy and loneliness can occupy the same square meter. Subject Sue’s Details In The Dark feels built for the hour when the club has stopped pretending to be a social space and has become something more private, a room full of people moving beside one another while each carries a separate crisis under the skin. The Amsterdam artist works in that unstable zone between desire and estrangement, where a glance across the floor can feel intimate for thirty seconds and absurdly remote by the time the bass turns over again. Across six tracks, Sue treats darkwave and ethereal techno less as genres than as materials she can bend around a voice that never sounds entirely convinced by the scene surrounding it. The synthesizers are dense without turning blunt, the percussion keeps its discipline, and the vocals drift above the machinery with a cool distance that makes every romantic gesture feel temporary. There is pleasure everywhere, though it comes with the suspicion that pleasure has already started charging interest. In Details In The Dark, synth lines stretch wide, then recede; voices stack until they resemble memories arguing over the same event; beats keep moving with the indifferent authority of a machine that has seen a thousand romances begin and collapse before breakfast. Sue’s music carries the cold poise of Boy Harsher or Minuit Machine, but her own instinct leans more toward psychological ambiguity than brute force. She seems fascinated by the gap between what happened, what was wanted, and what gets remembered later. The best moments make uncertainty itself feel physical, a pressure in the chest that still leaves room for dancing. The accompanying video sharpens that idea by turning Sue into a modern Louise Brooks wandering through a glitch-struck universe that seems detached from ordinary chronology. Her severe bob and silent-era poise collide with digital ruptures, warped space, and fractured movement, giving the clip the look of a lost screen goddess accidentally uploaded into a corrupted future. items.body: I've read other reviews of Dreadnought's upcoming release and they've described the album as more "direct". I don't know if I necessarily agree or, rather, if I think that's the main that should be highlighted. To be sure, Wars of Spirit // Wards of Light (from here on called Wars) is more direct in the sense that the more ethereal passages of previous Dreadnought releases are mostly gone. All tracks clock in under ten minutes and their structure is a bit more straight forward in how it balances the psychedelic, "lighter" elements of Dreadnought's sound and the more vociferous, black metal sound.But there's a deeper transformation for the band's sound on Wars that I think merits focus and that's a sea change in the entire palette of Dreadnought on this release. On previous releases, all the way back to Bridging Realms, Dreadnought lived on a tight rope; the band were constantly balancing those two modes I referenced above. Emergence was perhaps the exception and therefore the album which sounds the most like Wars; like it, Emergence had a more rumbling, bass-forward sound and tended to "explode" less into that other, treble and tenor focused mode of Dreadnought. Wars is very much the same, more contemplative, "richer", less prone to far flung gestures, and more dedicated to a thicker, more present sort of approach.Which is not to say it never explodes; it does. But check out the way in which it does, on opening track "Tiamat's Gate" five minute mark. In the past, this passage (the catharsis of the track) would have been accompanied by high-pitched screams, whirling float, and punctual piano. But here, the center of the weight is focused on a maelstrom like guitar riff, embellished by deep, sonorous riffs and, of course, Kelly Schilling's powerful vocals. But they are more of the "haggard" variety, with that unique timbre she has. And they trade places with a much deeper growl provided by Ryan Sims. The end result is a darker, more brooding sound. Yes, Schilling's familiar clean vocals come in later and yes, the track winds into a soaring peak. But then it's also immediately snatched into a gorgeous, muted passage punctuated by excellently restrained blast beats, darkly scintillating synths, and deep, subtle bass.This new iteration on the sound continues through the release: the synths sound fuller but also more contemplative and atmospheric for example. You can hear that on "Aeonwar", where they basically good full darkwave in their sound (beautifully melded with Schilling's gothic style). Likewise the guitars continue to be denser and thicker than before, less worried about tracing every peak and crescendo and more focused on creating texture and weight to the sound. It's on full display for "Aeonwar", with one of my favorite riffs from the band's history doing wonders "beneath" the gossamer synths. It's Dreadnought, for sure, and it's made up of the elements which first caused me to fall in love with the band. But most importantly, it champions the quality which I love Dreadnought the most for: change. Wars of Spirit // Wards of Light is a further step in the band's career, deeper into the beating, shadowed heart of their sound. Wars of Spirit // Wards of Light by Dreadnought

items.body: ドイツの音楽家、ラルフ・ハイデルが日本で初のコンサートを開催（2026年10月6日、ルーテル市ヶ谷ホールにて実施）する。ラルフ・ハイデルはベルリン在住のミュージシャン。作曲家として、またマルチ楽器奏者として、サックスやフルート、クラリネット、ピアノ、シンセサイザーなどを操り、ジャズやクラシック、現代音楽を横断する作品を生み出している。 そんな偉才の初来日公演を企画したのは、日本のデザインスタジオ、upcoming.studio（アップカミングスタジオ）である。音楽ビジネスとは無縁の彼らが、なぜベルリン在住の音楽家と連携し、初来日公演をプロデュースするに至ったのか。そして、一体どんなステージになるのか。 ベルリンのラルフ・ハイデルと、東京の upcoming.studio（孫兆軒さん／マッカートニー龍馬さん）をオンラインでつなぎ、その経緯を聞いた。 SNSのメッセージから来日公演へ ──そもそも、どんな経緯でこのプロジェクトは始動したのですか？ 孫兆軒（以下：孫） 僕とマッカートニーは、東京都内でデザインスタジオを運営していまして。2人とも音楽が好きなので、よく情報交換をするんです。それで、最近聴いたラルフ・ハイデルの『anyways.onto better things』が良かった、という話になって。 ──あのアルバムは2025年の発表でしたね。 孫 そうです。ちょうど１年くらい前。僕は「春の雨」というレコードショップのSNSでラルフの存在を知って。めちゃくちゃいいサウンドだと思ってすぐにアナログ盤を買いました。で、そのレコードをマッカートニーが見て「俺もそれ買った。めっちゃいいよね」って。 マッカートニー龍馬（以下：龍馬） そんな話の流れで、ラルフのインスタグラムを見つけて「あなたのアルバムは最高だ」とコメントしたんです。するとラルフから「君はどこで何をやっている人なの？」という返信が来ました（笑）。それで、僕は日本で活動しているデザイナーで…みたいな感じで自己紹介して。 ラルフ・ハイデル （以下：ラルフ） 僕はその頃ちょうど「日本でライブをやりたいな…」と思っていた時期だったので、そのことを彼らに伝えました。でも、どこで演奏できるのか分からないし、誰を頼ればいいのかもわからない。そんな話をしたことが、今回のプロジェクトのはじまりです。 孫 それで、僕らの知り合いでライブをオーガナイズできる人を探して、一度ミーティングをしよう、ということになりました。でも話しているうちに「これもう、自分たちでやろうか」という方向へどんどん進んでいきました。 ──ラルフさんはなぜ日本でコンサートをやりたいと思ったのですか？ ラルフ 僕は以前にプライベートな旅行で日本を訪れたことがあります。そのときに、いろんなレコードショップや音楽的な場所にも行きました。そして、僕の音楽を好きだと言ってくれる人たちにも会うことができた。自分の音楽が、遠い日本の人たちに響いていることはすごく嬉しかったし、なんだか不思議な感覚でした。それで、「いつかここで演奏したい」と思うようになりました。 さっき彼らの話にも出たけれど、東京の「春の雨」というレコード店が僕のレコードを扱ってくれました。最初は５枚くらい渡して、それから２週間後に「もっと送ってほしい」と連絡が来たんです。すぐに追加で15枚を送り、そのあとさらに15枚といった具合にどんどん増えていった。とても自然な流れで、口コミで広がっていったのだと感じました。 日本独特の「音楽鑑賞」文化 ──日本のリスナーに響いた理由は何だと思いますか？ ラルフ 以前に僕が出したアルバム『anyways.onto better things』で、三宅純さんが参加してくれました。そのことは僕が日本のファンに気づいてもらえる大きなきっかけになったと思います。 もうひとつ付け加えるなら、日本にはアンビエント・ミュージックの長い伝統があります。僕自身はアンビエントを専門につくっているわけではありませんが、その伝統があるからこそ、僕のような音楽に対する理解も深いのだと思います。 日本の皆さんは、アナログな温かい音色や古い楽器と、現代テクノロジーを融合させる僕のスタイルを評価してくれていると感じます。それは、伝統的な要素と非常に高度なテクノロジーが同時に存在している日本という国にも重なります。 ──あなたの音楽にはアンビエント的な側面もありますが、ジャズやクラシックの素養も活かしつつ、独創的な表現を編み出してしますね。 ラルフ 最近ではジャズのアーティストも新しい領域をどんどん開拓しています。そうした音楽は複雑さや難解さもあって孤立しがちです。でも日本では違う。多くの人が集うような場所で、複雑で奥深い音楽が流れていて皆それを楽しんでいます。 もちろんヨーロッパにもそうした音楽が聴ける場所はありますが、東京はより自然で日常的にそうした音楽を楽しめる環境が整っている。 ──なかでも特に心を惹かれた場所や現象はありますか？ ラルフ リスニングバーです。これは非常に豊かな、日本の文化のひとつだと思う。そこはコンサートホールやライブハウスではない。けれど人々は音楽を聴くためにその空間へ集まって、音を聴くことに強く集中している。そんな場所や催しはヨーロッパではあまり見かけません。僕が日本を観光したとき、まずそのことに驚いたし、本当に素晴らしい環境だと思いました。 「人生最高のライブ」を求めて ──最新アルバム『Live at silent green Berlin』について伺います。これはどういう内容の作品ですか？ ラルフ さっき話に出たアルバム『anyways.onto better things』のリリース・コンサートを収録したものです。ベルリンにあるサイレント・グリーンというホールで行ったライブ録音です。当然ですが、スタジオアルバムとは少し違います。即興演奏の比率が多く、よりジャズ的で、エネルギーもずっと強い。 ──このライブは、サックス奏者のモリッツ・シュタール（Moritz Stahl）と、ドラマーのダニ・シェフェルズ（Dani Scheffels）とのトリオ編成でしたね。 ラルフ そう、私はピアノとシンセサイザー、ボーカル、サックスを担当しました。あの日は会場の雰囲気も信じられないほど素晴らしかった。僕たちが中央で演奏し、観客がその周りを囲むように座っている。本当に美しいコンサートで、僕の人生のなかで最高のライブのひとつです。   ──今回の日本公演も録音作品になる可能性もありますか？ ラルフ そうなるくらい素晴らしい内容になることを願っています。 ──今回はバンド形態ではなく、ソロ公演です。どんな内容を想定していますか？ ラルフ もちろん、魔法のような瞬間をあらかじめ計画することはできません。ただ、僕にとって非常に特別な公演です。日本で演奏するのは初めてだし、初公演としては比較的大きな規模なので、まだ発表していない作品や誰も聴いたことのない曲も演奏するつもりです。 楽器はピアノ、サックス、シンセサイザーが中心になります。それぞれの楽器に、しっかりと焦点を当てられる構成が好きなんです。それから、会場にとても美しいグランドピアノがあるので、それも生かしたい。 デザインスタジオと音楽家のセッション 龍馬 僕らはブッキングのプロではないし、音楽や興行に関しても素人です。そんな人間と仕事をするのは、プロのミュージシャンにとって大きなリスクだと思います。きちんとブッキングできるのか、そもそも本当に信頼できるのか。そこはラルフも心配だったんじゃないかな。 ラルフ いや、僕はいつも音楽業界の外側にも目を向けるようにしているので、アップカミングスタジオとの連携は自分にとって自然な流れだった。そもそも僕自身がすべてDIYだからね。自分のレーベルを立ち上げ、ディストリビューションも自分でやって、レコードも自分でプレスし、ドイツ国内のライブも自分でブッキングしている。 もちろん、その過程で音楽業界のいろんな人と接触し、一緒に仕事をすることもあります。ただ僕にとって、一緒に仕事をする相手が音楽業界にいるかどうかは重要なことではありません。相手に対してポジティブな感覚を持てたら、僕はその人と一緒にやってみます。そういうときにこそ、型にはまらない、おもしろい結果が得られるから。 ──デザインスタジオならではの強みもありますね。 孫 僕たちはコンサートを制作した経験はありませんが、デザインスタジオとして培ってきた別の経験があります。それから、僕らは一人の音楽ファンとして、いろいろなライブへ行ってきました。そんな中で「ここが良かった」と感じることもあるし「ここが残念だったな」と思うこともあります。例えば、音楽と会場がマッチしていなかったり、演出や進行が適切でなかったり。そうしたストレスのない、気配りの効いたコンサートにしたいです。 龍馬 音だけでなく視覚も大切だし、なによりそのライブが「体験として素晴らしかった」と感じてもらえることが大切です。まずはそういう環境をつくる。その前提ができたときに、ラルフがどんなモチベーションで、どんなコンサートをするのか。僕らも楽しみにしています。そこは、ある意味で僕らとラルフとのセッションだと思っています。 ラルフ 彼らアップカミングスタジオとその周りにある世界を見たとき、そのシーンの中ですでに僕の音楽を聴いて理解してくれている人たちがいた。それは僕にとって、とても重要なことでした。 僕自身も彼らの作品がとても好きですし、すでに別のプロジェクトでも一緒に仕事をしました。だから今回の決断は、とても自然で、前向きなものでした。 ──このコンサート以外にも、すでに進行しているプロジェクトがあるのですか？ 龍馬 ファッションブランドの映像作品でラルフに音楽を依頼しました。知り合いの映像監督が映像を撮り、孫がディレクションに入り、ラルフに音楽をつくってもらいました。 その作品の仕上がりも良かったし、実際に一度仕事をしたことで互いの信頼も深まりました。映像監督もラルフの音楽をとても気に入って、来日時にミュージックビデオを撮りたいという話にまで広がっています。 孫 単にラルフを日本へ呼ぶだけではなく、セッションのように一緒に作品や機会をつくっていく。そういう仕事の仕方は、今回に限らず僕らの活動の根っこにあります。今回、それが実現していることをうれしく思っています。 いわゆる “音楽業界” の中だけで完結させない、日本のさまざまなクリエイティブやほかの業界にとも繋がって、そこへきちんと還元されるようなイベントにしたいです。 ラルフ 僕は今回の来日公演まで、しばらくヨーロッパでもライブを行わない予定です。フレッシュな状態で新しい音楽を演奏できることを楽しみにしています。僕にとって、本当に特別な公演になると思います。 Ralph Heidel in Tokyo 日時：2026年10月6日（開場 18:30／開演 19:30） 会場：ルーテル市ヶ谷ホール Tickets – 全席指定席 – ZAIKO, イープラスにて販売受付中 主催：upcoming.studio 音響設計：Motoki Moky Tanizawa 制作協力：朝河電気 広報協力：春の雨 cafe & records 助成：アーツカウンシル東京［東京芸術文化創造発信助成（単年助成）］芸術創造活動 投稿 【ラルフ・ハイデル】初来日コンサート直前インタビュー｜日本のデザインスタジオと連携して待望の初来日公演を実現 は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items._cn_summary: 本次访谈围绕拉尔夫·海德尔的创作与首次日本公演展开。他是一位横跨爵士、古典、现代音乐与电子领域的柏林音乐家，擅长萨克斯、钢琴、合成器等多种乐器。其作品注重原声乐器与电子技术的融合，带有明显的即兴性和氛围感。专辑《anyways.onto better things》通过东京唱片店的口碑传播获得日本听众关注，最新现场专辑记录了柏林演出的即兴与爵士能量。此次日本公演将以钢琴、萨克斯、合成器为中心，并包含未发行作品，呈现更接近即兴演奏的现场体验。
