items.body: Taimela isn’t trying to recreate the 90s IDM and drum and bass golden era so much as he’s drawing a line from it to the present, letting those influences inform his melodic instincts without being consumed by them. There’s a lightness to how he carries all of that reference—it never feels like homework, never feels like pastiche. It just sounds like a producer who grew up on the right records and internalized them so completely that they became his own vocabulary. Very thought out melodically, nostalgic at times, and beautifully crafted Cheap Ingredients by Otto Taimela   Finland has a particular relationship with electronic music that rarely gets the credit it deserves. The same quiet introspection that runs through the country’s classical and folk traditions has found its way into a generation of producers who make IDM and ambient work that feels rooted in landscape and weather rather than dancefloors or scenes. Otto Taimela is one of the most versatile of them—a pianist, composer, sound designer, and producer based in Finland with a discography that refuses categorization, moving between avant-garde piano, breakbeat, ambient techno, and neo-classical composition across labels like SWIMS, Cold Blow, Ultraääni, Special Species Records, and Cudighi Records, the LA-based label run by Ben Van Howe that focuses on international psych, art pop, ambient, and electronic music. This is Taimela‘s second release on Cudighi following 2024’s A Life, and it’s the most coherent statement of his IDM-facing side yet. Cheap Ingredients is a good IDM release and a genuinely cute one—cute in the sense that the sounds and melodies composed through this album are lovely, catchy, and beautiful to listen to. The album plays consistently well as a flow of old-school breakbeats and drum styles with beautiful pads and keys throughout. As uncanny as the cover looks, what appears to be two Mickey Mouse-like characters standing next to a palm tree, drawn in a deliberately naive hand, it doesn’t match the aesthetic of the music at all, which makes it strangely interesting. The music overall sounds very thought out melodically, nostalgic at times, and beautifully crafted. The genre here sits closer to drum and bass IDM than anything else—not drill and bass, which is more aggressive and abstract in structure, and not liquid drum and bass, which is softer and more melodic in the conventional sense. This has an abstract structure to it while maintaining real warmth in the low end subs. “VCXO” is a prime example of good bass sub usage and chill, not too fast, not too slow, just good downtempo electronica. The melodies and atmospheres here hit somewhere between Roni Size‘s early drum and bass work and the melodic sensibility of Plaid, two reference points that don’t often share the same sentence but make complete sense here. Standouts: “Glacier,” “New Life,” “Spell 3,” and “Formal Mass.” “Spell 3” is particularly hypnotizing in its ambience and loop, it recalls the old school Boards of Canada loops that take you off guard, the kind that don’t announce themselves as special until you realize you’ve been inside them for longer than you expected. “Bullfinch Nest” exposes beautiful vocal warble work coming in every four to eight bars, it sounds like a bird, or the reminiscence of one, and when the pads arrive alongside it the combination becomes catchy in a way that’s hard to shake. Whatever that sample is, it’s the character of the track. It recalls Aphex Twin‘s “Slow Bird Whistle” from the Peel Sessions in concept — not in sound, not in execution, but in the specific idea of a non-musical element becoming the personality of a piece. Very well done. “Mysterious Thing” is a wonderful interlude, the vocal sample and record-rewinding effect being tossed into the playing melody is fantastic to listen to. It’s not turntablism—it’s something closer to the small, playful interludes that appeared on early Plaid releases, or the kind of moment that Mr. Oizo delivered on Analog Worms Attack (1999)—those brief, almost comedic left turns that humanize an otherwise electronic record. This would be the drum and bass version of that instinct, and it works perfectly. The album grows on you with each listen. It really is hard to choose between tracks because the more time you spend with it the more it reveals. A golden egg of classic sounds and nostalgia, one of those releases that knows exactly what era it’s drawing from and has the skill to make it feel fresh rather than imitative. Taimela isn’t trying to recreate the 90s IDM and drum and bass golden era so much as he’s drawing a line from it to the present, letting those influences inform his melodic instincts without being consumed by them. There’s a lightness to how he carries all of that reference—it never feels like homework, never feels like pastiche. It just sounds like a producer who grew up on the right records and internalized them so completely that they became his own vocabulary. Cheap Ingredients is exactly what the title doesn’t suggest—carefully considered, melodically rich, and worth every return listen. Cheap Ingredients is available on Cudighi. [Bandcamp] The post Otto Taimela :: Cheap Ingredients (Cudighi) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 芬兰制作人Otto Taimela在专辑中并未简单复刻90年代IDM与鼓打贝斯的黄金时代，而是将那些影响内化为个人语汇，以轻盈的姿态连接过去与现在。作品兼具抽象结构与温暖低频，旋律编排精心，带有怀旧气息却不流于模仿。专辑在旧式碎拍与优美键盘、垫底音色之间取得平衡，既有Roni Size早期作品的低音质感，也带有Plaid式的旋律敏感度。整体听感流畅，适合沉浸式聆听，是Taimela面向IDM风格最为连贯的一次表达。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Some 36 years in and still going strong. The now legendary SIGH has become nearly synonymous withJapanese avant-garde metal with a knack for melding the most unlikely of sounds together in acohesive whole and still finding new ways to take the fanbase somewhere the band has not yetexplored. Once again the crazed black metal turned experimental sonic wizards led by the inimitableMirai Kawashima returns with its 14th release GOH-KA, another hi-brow conceptual masterwork thattranslates as something akin to "infernal fire scorching the sinners" or simply "karma." The albumdelves into the darker concepts of Buddhism including the concepts adapted from the Buddhist hellscrolls and through a series of 11 tracks this team of five presents a fiery hellish journey thatforges a fiery path through the crossroads of bands such as Celtic Frost, Voivod, second wave blackmetal and traditional Japanese music.It's the usual maelstrom of anything goes in the SIGH universe although GOH-KA retains the morefocused approach of tightly woven concept albums of recent years. You can expect the usualthunderous roar of black metal guitar works along with a pounding bass and drum accompaniment butSIGH delves deep into its Japanese heritage with ample traditional instruments woven into the mixalong with moments that eschew the metal paradigm completely with large chunks of "Anzenshokon" forexample sounding more like a movie soundtrack before trading off with the first wave black metalapproach that has been its bailiwick since its inception. Joining the SIGH team is bassist Fr�d�ricLeclercq (Kreator, Dragonforce), ex-Fear Factory drummer Mike Heller and Opeth mastermind Mikael�kerfeldt who delivers a ripping guitar solo on "Unputenpu" the album's lead single.SIGH traverses these brackish waters well and with the opening "Kuso-shi (1-3)" runs the gamut ofcrafty psychedelic rock laced avant-metal with epic classic Japanese traditionals interwoven into araspy narrative that together generate interesting melodic developments, stylish fusionfunctionality and epic transitions between varying stylistic approaches. Perhaps a mellower lessmetal dependent release from previous works but an effective expansion of the sonic palette whereatmospheric embellishments are allowed to shine like diamonds in the rough. The one constant that isthe thread between all SIGH albums are the raspy vocals of Kawashima's feisty spirited lyricaldelivers however there are many more backing vocal additions which give this album a much largerthan life production value. As always many metal purists may not deem GOH-KA as metal enough butlike many of SIGH's constructs, the metal is merely one vital ingredient to a much larger sonicedifice. Somewhat reminiscent of the band's best known release "Imaginary Soundscape," GOH-KA delivers asimilar kaleidoscopic approach where psychedelia, metal, traditional folk and progressive symphonicrock play together like Bambi and Godzilla in a universe of the band's own making and once againsomehow despite all the odds stacked against the whole shebang comes off as yet another triumphantvictory for this Tokyo based band that continues to punctuate the 21st century with some of the mostcutting edge sounds under the greater banner of metal music. Personally i find the expanded use oftraditional Japanese instruments and homegrown flavors to be the wise choice for this creative bandto delve into. Metal and folk music has been immensely popular for over three decades now but yetthe Japanese have been more reticent to traverse these developments however SIGH proves it has thechops to pull it all off with ease. Another excellent release from Tokyo's wildest metal band.

items._cn_summary: SIGH 第十四张专辑以佛教地狱概念为线索，将黑金属、前卫摇滚与传统日本乐器编织成一幅烈火般的音景。专辑延续乐队一贯的杂食风格，在凯尔特霜、Voivod 与第二波黑金属的骨架上加入尺八、筝等东方声响，部分段落甚至脱离金属框架，呈现出近似电影配乐的氛围织体。制作层面邀请了 Kreator、Dragonforce 的贝斯手 Fr�d�ric Leclercq、ex-Fear Factory 鼓手 Mike Heller 及 Opeth 核心 Mikael �kerfeldt 献艺，阵容多元。主唱川岛的三浦式沙哑嗓音依然是贯穿线索，但大量和声叠加使整体音场更为宏大。相比前作，这张作品更偏内敛，金属比重降低，氛围与即兴段落得以舒展，呈现出类似《Imaginary Soundscape》的万花筒式拼贴美学。

items.body: In the spring, Eric van Wonterghem returned with a new album from his Monolith project—the sonic alter ego he launched nearly thirty years ago. For the first time, he is releasing a Monolith album on his own label. Yama is the Hindu god of death and justice, responsible for administering justice and punishing sinners; this theme inspired the album’s ten tracks, at least in the digital version. Monolith remains true to the unique and instantly recognizable sound van Wonterghem has cultivated over the years. It is a precise fusion of Tribal rhythms, Industrial sounds, and Trance-like build-ups. The album as a whole—especially the harder tracks—is highly driving and danceable, culminating in a genuine Trance climax. At the same time, calmer, more atmospheric tracks provide welcome variety while still making a distinct impact on the listener. This is largely due to the remarkable atmosphere Monolith creates once again. Another essential element of the project’s signature sound is the Eastern vibe that permeates the tracks and fits the album’s concept perfectly. Eric van Wonterghem remains a true sound guru, particularly when it comes to the icy tones he weaves into his loops. I am also completely captivated by the deep, overwhelming and explosive bass sounds that anchor the tracks and pair perfectly with the driving rhythms. Monolith has never let me down. This Belgian pioneer once more manages to amaze and convince me. In short, another unmissable album. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Shiva”: Shiva by Monolith About Monolith Monolith is the solo project of Belgian musician Eric van Wonterghem, set up in 1997. Van Wonterghem has also worked with Absolute Body Control, The Klinik, Insekt, Sonar, and Detune-X, and has contributed to Dive album productions. The project built its reputation on a Tribal-Industrial sound, a fusion of Tribal percussion, Industrial production, and Trance-style builds that van Wonterghem has continued to refine across more than a decade of releases. In 2016, Monolith released the four-track EP “Time Running Out” (“Construct”, “De-construct”, “Ghost Cities”, and “Time”) on Sonic Groove, later issued on vinyl. The project also runs its own Bandcamp imprint, SoundOfMonolith, used in 2020 to self-release “The Disco Buddha Variations”, new edits of a track van Wonterghem has described as one of his best-known pieces. Van Wonterghem released his eleventh Monolith album, “Unnatural Bodies”, on Hands in 2020, describing the record as an attempt to make “art without rules” inspired by the mechanical-organic sculptures of artist Jim Whiting. He discussed the approach in a 2020 interview with Side-Line. “Yama”, released on van Wonterghem’s own label Prodam Records, is the first Monolith album issued through his own imprint. The digital edition holds ten tracks built around the album’s theme, the Hindu god of death and justice.

items.body: Veronica & the Dark Particles sound as though somebody fed a goth club into a deep-space transmitter, waited for the machine to malfunction, and discovered the malfunction had better bass than the original program. Initial Transmission, the Florida duo’s debut album, comes loaded with retro-futurist synths, rigid post-punk bass, hard electronic percussion, and Veronica Blak’s cool, velvet-toned delivery moving through the machinery with the calm of someone who has already seen the catastrophe beyond the airlock. British composer Eniac Nine gives these eight tracks weight. The bass is thick without turning muddy, the drums land with mechanical discipline, and the synthesizers occupy a wide field that can suddenly feel enormous without losing definition. Blak sits removed from the center of the mix, suited to lyrics preoccupied with obsession, dread, distortion, paralysis, and the queasy suspicion that technology has learned more about us than we have learned about ourselves. “Eniac Nine and I never worked together before but he brought me such a compelling collection of diverse tracks that the lyrics and melodies formed almost instantly in my head,” says Blak. “I like the unique sounds he crafts for each song like a spaceship door opening in Digital or Indian tabla inspired drums on Monster that you don’t hear in modern darkwave.” Liquify begins with an electronic throb that feels clinical, almost chemical, its bass moving with the slow certainty of something spreading through the bloodstream. Small synthetic details hover around the beat while Blak’s voice supplies the human temperature, cool and controlled even as the arrangement grows more claustrophobic. Digital is stranger and more playful, crawling forward on a crooked, slinky rhythm that recalls Strange Boutique launched several thousand miles beyond Earth. Synthetic noises open and close around the song like mechanical doors, giving its groove the peculiar sensation of wandering through some abandoned pleasure station where the computers have kept the music running after the passengers disappeared. Monster throws subtlety aside for speed and impact, propelled by tabla-inspired percussion, hard electronic drums, and one of the album’s biggest hooks. Blak rides above the commotion with enough authority to make the chorus feel ready for collective shouting in a packed club. Rumors lowers the temperature and gives anxiety room to multiply. Its slower movement produces a particular kind of paranoia, where every empty measure seems capable of concealing another piece of bad information. The scale feels enormous without sacrificing intimacy, turning private suspicion into something closer to societal collapse viewed through a bedroom window. Dunes ventures much farther outside conventional darkwave coordinates. Strange synthetic tones, threatening low frequencies, and a cinematic sense of distance suggest some hostile future civilization whose architecture was designed without human comfort in mind. Lost retreats into more recognizably European coldwave territory, recalling Clan of Xymox and Lebanon Hanover through its severe bass movement and unusual pockets of echo. Voices and instruments seem displaced from one another, as though the song were being heard simultaneously from several adjoining rooms. Then comes The Kiss, their treatment of The Cure’s 1987 classic, trimmed into a tighter form with an unexpectedly sharp pop instinct. Robert Smith’s original recording sprawls through obsession until guitar becomes nearly physical pressure; Veronica & the Dark Particles concentrate that fever into a more economical attack. The bass carries much of the psychological weight, while Blak approaches the lyric with a colder sensuality that makes its possessiveness feel calculated rather than delirious. Closing track Rings widens everything again, bringing broad synthesizer passages and space-rock scale into the album’s final stretch. After seven songs spent probing machines, desire, fear, and psychological contamination, the record ends staring outward into an expanse too large to explain, sending its final signal into whatever might be listening. Listen to Initial Transmission below and order the album here. Initial Transmission by Veronica & the Dark Particles “I don’t like single sounds, I like to mix things together to intentionally create complex layers like stacking monosyths,” says Nine. “I write music almost daily, visualizing the texture of sound like a wave table. I don’t rely on samples or loops because I am compelled to craft a universe of unique elements.” That philosophy explains why Initial Transmission works best when its surfaces collide: club music with gothic reserve, machine order with psychological unease, elegance with menace. Veronica & the Dark Particles have made a debut built for black rooms, highway drives after midnight, and the uneasy pleasure of dancing while the future looks increasingly untrustworthy. items.body: The mind protects itself by hiding what it cannot yet bear to see. Trauma may become a locked room whose very door triggers fear. Denial, dissociation, and avoidance are not proof of hidden programming, but ways consciousness narrows around pain until, with safety, the forbidden room can be approached again. Planeswalkers begin their odyssey with an unusually literal name. The collaboration between gothic songstress Arden Leigh and electronic composer Andrew Means takes its title from the occult idea of moving consciousness between planes through dreams, trance, meditation, astral projection, or other altered states. Their debut EP, The Mind Room, turns that metaphysical vocabulary toward trauma, dissociation, memory, and recovery, imagining the psyche as a series of sealed chambers approached indirectly when direct confrontation feels overwhelming. The record’s premise draws on Leigh’s belief that extreme trauma can create psychological “tripwires,” while denial and avoidance may become forms of protection. Such language carries obvious clinical and spiritual complications, yet The Mind Room is most persuasive when it translates those ideas into texture and movement rather than explanation. Leigh describes the partnership in explicitly occult terms: “Andrew is a really skilled psychic, one of the best I’ve ever met, and he predicted that we’d have more success with it this way. I got a third-party divination just to be sure, and sure enough, it said he was right. We decided to name ourselves Planeswalkers after our shared occult hobbies…I’d say Andrew is a lot better at planeswalking than I am, but I get the job done when needed, or I compensate for it with other aspects of my practice. There were times when we’d finish working on music and then lie down on my floor and astral project together. It’s a really amazing gift to have met someone who shares my two main interests of music and magick like that, and I’m really looking forward to seeing how we continue to explore both of them as we keep working together.” Across four tracks, The Mind Room treats psychic exploration as both subject and compositional principle. The rooms keep changing shape, and the record’s deepest question remains simple: how does someone approach what the mind has placed behind a locked door? Horizons opens amid static, distant electronics, and gentle cymbals. Leigh’s voice floats high above the arrangement with an Enya-like purity, making the track resemble a guided meditation intercepted by an unstable transmission. Its spacious trip-hop architecture recalls Massive Attack, though ruptures of noise repeatedly disturb the calm. Clockwork gives the EP firmer physical dimensions. Leigh’s commanding register suggests Zola Jesus, while Means bends electronic tones into an uncanny interior where corridors seem to extend past their logical endpoints. Repetition becomes claustrophobic, and the title begins to feel mechanical in the psychological sense: a mind caught inside patterns that continue moving after conscious control has weakened. Body makes the sharpest turn. Trip-hop drums support a leering chant, voices push toward shouting, and the earlier inward drift acquires force. The lyric about “walking the planes” supplies the duo with their name, but the song remains intensely corporeal, concerned with breath, rhythm, threat, and will. The closing Alive returns to open space and echo, with Leigh’s voice receding and reappearing as though consciousness were adjusting to gravity after an excursion elsewhere. Order The Mind Room here and listen below: “For resources on plurality, including traumagenic DID, or to make a donation, we recommend supporting The Plural Association here,” suggest the band. items._cn_summary: Planeswalkers的首张EP《The Mind Room》以形而上学词汇切入创伤、记忆与意识修复的主题，由哥特歌手Arden Leigh与电子作曲家Andrew Means合作完成。四首曲目将心灵探索转化为作曲原则，声音空间不断变形重组。开篇曲《Horizons》在静电与远距电子声中铺陈，Leigh的声音高悬于编排之上，带有Enya般的纯净感，整体架构令人联想到Massive Attack的trip-hop美学，不时有噪音裂隙打破平静。《Clockwork》则赋予EP更坚实的物理维度，Leigh的声线展现出Zola Jesus般的威严感，Means将电子音色弯折成超现实的内向空间，重复段落渐趋幽闭，标题本身暗含机械化的心理学隐喻。评论将这张作品视为对封闭心室如何被间接接近这一核心命题的持续追问。

items.body: For a few years, I have had this funny vision of Antwerp’s Summer Bummer festival taking place on a beach near a body of water. I had sunshine, seagull calls and good vibes in this fantasy. In reality, the venue, a rock club called Trix, is located on a busy road amongst high-rise apartment buildings just outside of downtown Antwerp. So, no seagulls, no beach and even the sun was being fickle. It troubled me, what could be the source for this misconception? The only part I had right was the ‘good vibes’. From the moment the first band started up in the darkened main hall on Friday afternoon to the closing tones of a bass-clarinet and electronics show on the intimate cafe stage late Saturday night, there was always something to hear, records to dig, people to talk shop with, and art to make — hardly leaving time to lament the waning days of the summer. Within the compact time-frame, starting late afternoon and ending around midnight on Friday and Saturday, festival organizers Koen Vandenhout and Christel Kumpen ran a tight program. Concerts were lined-up one after the other with a short break built-in to give the 200+ audience a chance to eat some dinner without developing FOMO. Plus, the sets ping-ponged from the main hall side to the cafe side, so there was always a chance to hit the bar if desired. Between the two halls, merch tables were arranged on all sides, making it dangerous to the wallet to traverse the venue. Parent organization of the festival Sound in Motion’s own Dropa-Disc label was present, as well as a record dealer with a selection of rare taste and local radio station Radio Centraal. If one purchased a t-shirt, or happened to have an extra one on hand, he or she (more likely than not: he) could head into the screen printing workshop and make their own with a festival design. Additionally, set in an adjacent room, musicians Cath Roberts and Tullis Rennie invited festival goers to record and manipulate sounds in a laboratory of their own design. When the weather was cooperative, one could visit the courtyard to procure some homemade food. Alexander von Schlippenbach and Paal Nilssen-Love The Sound In Motion website has the tagline, “Adventurous Music and Things”, and since we have got the things part out of the way, let us talk adventurous music . Not just a free-jazz festival, Summer Bummer’s scope this year included several avant-noise and electronics acts along with some of the most exciting musicians working (primarily) in Europe today. There was something for everyone, for example the ear-bleedingly loud Integral , a quartet comprised of Julien Desprez (guitar), Claire Gapenne (electronics and vocals), Christine Abelnour (sax) and Lukas Koenig (drums) that went from beguiling to battering, to the opening act, Kabas Sun Dogs, a Belgian band who had invited Canadian saxophonist Karen Ng and guitarist Jonathan Horne for a slowly unfolding exploration of both understatement and spirited groove. Rodrigo Amado, Joelle Leandre and Gerald Cleaver Highlights festooned the program, including a first time duo of drummer Paal Nilssen-Love and the legendary pianist Alexander von Schlippenbach as well as new trio formed by Rodrigo Amado with bassist Joelle Leandre and drummer Gerald Cleaver . In the duo’s extended set, Schlippenbach performed a chain of melodic ideas and Thelonius Monk song snippets that Nilssen-Love challenged with closely attuned force and precision. After a cautious opening, the trio of Amado, Leandre and Cleaver edged their way into the set, gathering momentum to the findcommon ground, letting Amado release his powerful tenor, Leandre impress with speed and expressiveness, and Cleaver move seamlessly between texture and forceful pulse. Daughter, Daughter The formidable quartet of Daughter, Daughter, comprised of Camila Nebbia and Amalie Dahl (saxophones), Elizabeth Coudoux (cello) and Sun Mi Hong (drums), performed a blend of composition and free-jazz improvisation showcasing both individual contributions as well as whole group interactions. The Berlin formation Das B , featuring Mazen Kerbaj (trumpet), Magda Mayas (piano), Tony Buck (drums) and Mike Majkowski (bass) was given the designation as a “super group“ in the program and their set did not refute this. Ostensibly deconstructing John Coltrane’s A Love Supreme , the quartet engaged in an exploratory and expansive sound collage complete with a trumpet played via surgical tubing and prepared piano that made the acoustic sound electric. Arguably one of the strongest shows of the festival. Das B Additionally, percussionist and singer Maria Portugal presented her EROSÃO Septet (Lotte Anker and Angelika Niescier on saxes , Matthias M üller and Moritz Wesp on trombones , Carl Ludwig H übsch on tuba and Reza Askari on bass ) , which performed a set of mid-tempo songs, both self-penned and from Brazilian composers, laced with some spicy improvisations. The next day, Portugal appeared in an exceptional duo with pianist Marta Warelis . As opposed to the septet, in which the music was a presented in more traditional structures, the songs themselves were de-composed and integrated organically with the ideas flowing from the pianist whose gentle and spacious playing grew progressively more ferocious. Marta Warelis and Maria Portugal Rounding out the program were two bass clarinet focused sets and several quite noisy ones. Representing the louder side, in addition to the aforementioned Integral, were New Best Friends (featuring Ng and Horne along with bassist Aaron Lumley and drummer Nasim L-P Navarro), the duo of Laurentiu Cotac and Diana Miron, and Mopcut with Desprez, Koenig and electronicist/vocalist Audrey Chen. Of these three, New Best Friends balanced their clamorous impulses best with a flowing set of improvisations. Bookending the festival were two bass clarinet sets. On the first day, John McCowen explored the extended tonalities of the acoustic contra-bass clarinet, exploiting the instrument’s multiphonic capabilities. Closing the festival, Hanna De Backer , in collaboration with the electronics of Yves De Mey , extended her instrument’s sonic possibilities to the outer realms. Overall, a musically adventurous and enjoyable festival, and although quite satisfied, I was still bothered by one thing: my imaginary festival on a beach. So, after some detective work, I believe I finally pinpointed the source of my whimsical misconception. In 2019, Rodrigo Amado's The Attic released the album Summer Bummer , recorded at the festival in 2018 and whose cover is an image of three cut-out figures sitting on a beach under a cloudless blue sky, looking out at the ocean. I didn’t know I was so impressionable! Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
Ezz-thetics

a column by
Stuart Broomer




This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”   

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.

items.body: ‘You know, hyenas aren’t the bad ones…these days it’s humans you should fear’. Anbessa follows the life of Asalif, a 10-year-old boy living with his mother on the outskirts of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. While it’s technically a score to the 2019 documentary of the same name, Anbessa is musically and thematically strong enough to stand on its own two legs, much like Asalif himself. Anbessa marks Erik K Skodvin’s first solo work in years, and it’s also his first solo film score. Asalif is caught between the old and the new, the imposing monoliths of tradition set against the ever-rising dunes of modernism. Anbessa’s score helps Asalif; it is a friend. He must make sense of deep change, which is occurring all around him. Western capitalism and ‘progress’ (which benefits a select few rather than the local population, disguising itself through slogans and spin) is slowly seeping into his way of life, threatening his mother’s safety and the lives of others in the community. By transforming into a lion (‘anbessa’ in Amharic), Asalif is capable of fighting these outside forces, better understanding himself and protecting his heritage while maintaining some semblance of control against a capitalist invasion. Asalif is able to fight back against those who are trying to cast him out, and in this respect, Anbessa’s score is appropriately dark. It isn’t apparent in the first couple of seconds – where children are laughing and playing together – but thicker drones soon come to blot out the light of their youth, throwing literal shadows over them with the prospect of a towering condominium, constructed on Asalif’s farmland, leaving both himself and his mother with a mere tool shed and no water. And the growth will not stop there; there are plans afoot to redesign and redevelop the area, the buildings beginning to mushroom outwards until people like Asalif and his mother and his friends are long forgotten. Both the country and the company will be sure to slant and spin the development, boasting of prosperity, vital economic development, and progress, when in reality it is anything but. Asalif taps into a fantasy wherein he becomes a hero – a lion – and uses his imagination to fight back, and as he does so, the score transforms, too. Skodvin is able to capture Ethiopia through field recordings of voice, song, and the nation’s percussive flavours, adding a ferocious roar where necessary. Under the alias of Svarte Greiner and as one half of Deaf Center, Skodvin’s music has slanted into shadows. It checks the boxes of being both haunted and bleak, but the dark was splintered by an ache of beauty and a delicate exploration of what it means to be human. Skodvin swaps the cabin in the woods for Asalif’s hut, where a simple life off the grid is on the brink of being destroyed. The promise of a better life is often too good to be true; there are always ulterior motives, usually to the detriment of its citizens or those who were originally promised to prosper from new developments. The drones prowl around, and thrumming textures cut into the mix, chopping the air like the blades of an approaching helicopter. Asalif’s voice mingles with the sound of thunder, shaking the ground. The roots of a justified anger echo through an intense, vengeful synth, but there is hope, too. Asalif has suffered injuries, and there’s nothing more dangerous than a wounded lion, but with Anbessa’s message of hope and steely resolve, those wounds will, in the fullness of time, become battle scars. www.miasmah.com

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Erik K Skodvin为2019年纪录片《Anbessa》创作的配乐，讲述埃塞俄比亚亚的斯亚贝巴郊区少年Asalif在传统与现代冲突中通过幻想化身狮子对抗资本主义入侵的故事。Skodvin以Svarte Greiner及Deaf Center成员身份闻名，此作是其多年来的首张个人作品，也是首次独立担纲电影配乐。音乐运用田野录音捕捉埃塞俄比亚的人声、歌唱与打击元素，融入厚重的无人机音墙与暗色质感，将非洲本土声音与北欧暗潮氛围相结合。配乐从开头孩童嬉笑声逐渐被浓重低频遮蔽，象征现代化对传统生活的侵蚀。Skodvin用声音构建出从明到暗的过渡，既展现了埃塞俄比亚的文化肌理，也延续了他一贯的阴暗忧郁美学。

items.body: A slow, icy breath is wrapped in rapid phased pulses, then burned through with a welding torch. Odd interjections like stuttered breath, an oscillating chord and loud metallic whirring. Vague thumping and scraping, a single-note bass riff that develops into a squelchy syncopated melody beneath the warbling and swishing of a UFO laser battle. Clicking like cicadas, fragments of voices and brass and woodwind blare, an overheard telephone conversation while an orchestra warms up next door. Echoing, gleaming tones, erratic almost-rhythms swelling and crescendoing, harmony growing in complexity as the echoes overlap and interfere. Beware of the growling, heard briefly and intermittently, from the monster in the sewer. In “Frozen Refrains”, Bérangère Maximin has created an album steeped in the acousmatic tradition: a wealth of different tones seemingly detached from all notion of source or origin, existing for themselves in a variety of different patterns and combinations, sounding from nowhere before returning to the same. References to non-sonic objects in the above descriptions are almost always superficial and subjective. Yet what frequently emerges across the album’s seven tracks is a strong sense of musicality, by which I mean that concerns such as harmony, rhythm, structure, and intensity are given the same weight as timbre and spectral analysis. A particularly striking manifestation of this is the way in which certain elements from one piece are often repeated in the next one, a risky ploy that could’ve easily come across as lazy or overly repetitive, but in Maximin’s hands gives the album an organic sense of wholeness and of different ideas growing from the same root. This strategy of reuse also hints at the way the music dances on the threshold of familiarity, even as it severs the link between sounds and their sources. Despite the indescribable timbres of many of the sounds, there’s sometimes an uncanny sense of having heard them somewhere before. The most obvious example of this is the woman’s voice in ‘Les Boucles Rebelles’, which is chopped into fragments and frozen in loops mid-phrase or even mid-word. The editing is jarring, and yet somehow so reminiscent of a sound heard everywhere these days: the public mobile phone conversation, one half inaudible, the other half constantly fragmented and interrupted by the utterances of the unheard interlocutor. What I like most about “Frozen Refrains” is the continuity between and within pieces, the melodic bass riff, quiet drone, or repeating chord that forms a steady base for all the clatter and swoosh and helps the music leave a stronger impression than the ever-changing parade of disparate sounds that often characterises acousmatic music. There’s continuity too between the hermetic, sealed-in world of the studio, where nothing has a past, and the quotidian environment beyond where everything is the product of what went before it. Bérangère Maximin seems equally at home in either, and brings the two together in intimate and enthralling conversation. Frozen Refrains by Berangere Maximin Bérangère Maximin Atlas Realisations
items._cn_summary: 《Frozen Refrains》是一张根植于声学传统（acousmatic）的实验专辑，七首曲目围绕声音本体展开，拒绝将声音与原始来源直接关联，让音色脱离语义独立存在。评论指出，作品在和声、节奏、结构与张力等音乐性维度上与音色频谱分析获得同等关注，旋律化的贝斯线条、稳定的低音无人机或重复和弦在多变的声响碎片间充当骨架，使整体超越声学音乐常见的碎片化局限。专辑各曲之间存在素材复用与呼应，形成有机的整体生长感，而非简单的重复堆叠。人声被切片冻结于词句中途，模拟公共场合手机通话的碎片化体验，与作品的"熟悉又陌生"气质相呼应。从冰冷的呼吸到焊接般的灼烧质感，从UFO激光战斗般的嘶鸣到下水道怪物的低吼，声响层次极为丰富，适合对当代作曲与声音艺术有持续关注的听众。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国出生、驻扎肯尼亚的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo，携手八十三岁的肯尼亚传统歌手Ogoya Nengo共同录制。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打打击乐与套鼓构建电子化的节奏底层，而Nengo与Ratengo的人声则在传统肯尼亚dodo歌唱与即兴之间来回抛接。评论特别提到《Bara》一曲中反复的打击模式逐渐叠加4/4节拍、低音与木琴质感，合成的复合节奏几乎不被察觉地融入声部；《Sarah》则以Ratengo的主唱搭配Kacirek试探性的碎拍打击，扭曲的电子质感在声浪顶点切入。整张专辑呈现出传统根源与前卫电子之间罕见的对话深度，将非洲民间旋律转化为二十一世纪的声响实验。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑延续第一卷，收录圣多美和普林西比在1970至1980年代的Puxa音乐，融合了merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等来自非洲葡语国家及加勒比地区的节奏元素。尽管岛屿面积小、录音产业有限，但专辑中的15首曲目展现了多把吉他相互缠绕、人声与和声应答交织的丰富织体，形成极具律动感的舞曲声响。Puxa曾遭葡萄牙殖民者禁止，却依然存续并演变出独特面貌。合辑由独立厂牌Bongo Joe发行，记录了非洲音乐黄金时代中被忽视的边陲之声，兼具历史文献价值与现场舞池能量。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续挪威三重奏对外部声音探索的路径，但比起前作更贴近地面。开篇曲以挪威西部springleik舞曲为素材，高音萨克斯先呈示旋律，低音提琴与鼓提供节奏根基，随后模块合成器和颤音琴以叠录方式加入。三人的分工从未固定，低音提琴转而与萨克斯同度奏出旋律，鼓组把节奏打开，整体趋向更加自由的集体即兴。作品在保留北欧民间素材的同时，让原声乐器与电子音色互相渗透，声部边界不断移动。值得关注的是乐队如何在不依赖固定声部的情况下保持紧密的对话感，使每次重复都产生新的层次。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: An off-kilter rhythm out of West African highlife opens “Higher Levels”, and Bart Vervaeck‘s guitar threads thin microtonal lines through it that lean towards Malian desert blues, while Lieven Van Pée‘s bass bubbles beneath in a funk register. It is the second single from Collective Intelligence, the third album from Brussels quartet Echoes of Zoo, out on 2 October via Rebel Up! Records and Zephyrus Records. The quartet formed in 2018 around saxophonist and composer Nathan Daems, who also leads Ethio-jazz five-piece Black Flower. Vervaeck and drummer Falk Schrauwen play in Ghent psych-jazz collective Compro Oro, Van Pée in jazz trio De Beren Gieren. Since the 2019 EP First Provocations, through BREAKOUT in 2021 and Speech of Species in 2023, they have built a punk-edged psychedelic jazz on Middle Eastern microtonal melody and West African rhythm. Animals have set the terms for each record: BREAKOUT on the friction between humans and animals, Speech of Species on how species talk to one another, this one on how they move as a single body. The album’s second track is called “Wolf Pack Telepathy”, and Daems ties the “Higher Levels” title to the sophisticated ways animals communicate and coordinate as one, or “what we casually call telepathy, though that label says more about our own limits than what’s actually possible in nature.” Stream “Higher Levels” and pre-order Collective Intelligence HERE The post Daily Discovery: Echoes of Zoo – Higher Levels appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

Records 与 Zephyrus Records 联合发行，定位明确指向欧洲地下世界音乐与前卫爵士交汇处。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Goh-Ka by Sigh is another great step forward for the Japanese metal legends, bringing back their earlier more manic Avant Garde black metal and thrash styles and mixing it with their recent folk, melodic and progressive metal sound. More than likely inspired by the re-recording of their classic album Hangman's Hymn, it is a return to parts of their classic sound, but not losing their recent progressive output. As always, Mirai Kawashima's manic vocals are always the unique trademark of the band, and it goes very well with the many different paths this album takes. And some of the melodic guitar work on this is very impressive. I'd give this a high 7 to low 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Kusoshi, 1 2, & 3.

Uredda brings together Thighpaulsandra (vocals, synthesizers, piano, organ, mellotron), Mariagiulia Degli Amori
items.body: Uredda, a new Italian-based project built around members of Zu and Coil/Spiritualized veteran Thighpaulsandra, has released “All He Knows” as the first single from its debut album, “Nüwa Mends the Sky”. The album is due December 4 via House of Mythology on black and clear vinyl LP, CD digipak and digital formats. The single arrives with an official music video. Uredda brings together Thighpaulsandra (vocals, synthesizers, piano, organ, mellotron), Mariagiulia Degli Amori (vocals, percussion, electronics), Bruno Germano (guitars, vocals), Paolo Mongardi (drums, percussion, vocals) and Massimo Pupillo (bass, vocals). Pupillo and Mongardi are also members of the Roman instrumental trio Zu, while Thighpaulsandra previously played in Coil and Spiritualized. The band’s sound mixes electronics, new wave, post-punk, krautrock and drone. ‘Nüwa Mends the Sky’ due December 4 via House of Mythology “Nüwa Mends the Sky” holds five tracks: “All He Knows,” “Dress To The Right,” “Blonde Charger,” “Tāne Obelisk” and “From the Ivy Bowl.” Uredda’s own Bandcamp listing and label coverage of the announcement both describe this as the album’s complete tracklist. The official video for “All He Knows” was uploaded to House of Mythology’s YouTube channel. It can be watched below. Nüwa Mends the Sky by Uredda Speaking about the release of “All He Knows,” Pupillo stated: “All I know is that a world on the precipice has a desperate need for beauty. Not a shallow and only cosmetic glamour, but real beauty – one that incorporates and transforms our deepest anxieties and fears. The diamond is born in the lotus, but the lotus is born from the mud.” “Nüwa Mends the Sky” can be pre-ordered through the House of Mythology store. About Uredda Uredda formed in Italy in 2026 out of an unplanned studio session. Thighpaulsandra had traveled to the country for a solo performance when Massimo Pupillo and Paolo Mongardi, working on new material at guitarist Bruno Germano’s studio, invited him to join them. Mariagiulia Degli Amori completed the lineup, and the resulting sessions became “Nüwa Mends the Sky” without prior rehearsal or a fixed plan for a band. Thighpaulsandra, born Timothy Lewis, began working with Julian Cope’s touring band in the late 1980s before joining Spiritualized in 1997, where he stayed until 2008 and appeared on releases including “Let It Come Down” and “Amazing Grace.” In 1998 he joined Coil, performing on “Astral Disaster” and both volumes of “Musick to Play in the Dark” alongside Peter Christopherson and John Balance. He also records with Pupillo in the duo URUK, which has released two albums since 2017. Pupillo and Mongardi play together in Zu, the Rome-founded instrumental trio formed in 1997 that also includes Luca Mai on baritone saxophone; Mongardi joined Zu’s lineup in 2011. The name Uredda comes from the “Caso Amicizia” (“Friendship Case”), an Italian account of alleged contact between humans and beings known as W56 in Abruzzo between 1956 and the late 1970s, in which “Uredda” denoted the vital energy of love and friendship. With “All He Knows” out now and “Nüwa Mends the Sky” set for December 4, Uredda’s debut marks the first joint release from this Zu-Thighpaulsandra lineup.

The album marks a shift in his sound: the electric
items.body: Swedish composer David Granström has released the single “A Shadow Cast”, the opening track from his new album “Echoes of Impermanence,” due November 6 on XKatedral as a CD and digital release. “Echoes of Impermanence” is Granström’s fourth full-length, following “Ephemeris” (2016) and “A Distant Color, Secluded” (2019) on XKatedral, and “Empty Room” on Hallow Ground. The album marks a shift in his sound: the electric guitar enters his previously hermetic, minimalist compositions built from long-duration digital synthesis, pushing a riff-driven character to the surface that had stayed submerged in his earlier work. Granström recorded the album at Elektronmusikstudion EMS and in his own studio, with help from Mats Erlandsson, who also mastered the record. Long-time collaborator and XKatedral co-founder Maria W Horn guests on Hurdy-Gurdy on the title track, “Echoes of Impermanence.” Granström plays guitar, synthesizers, zither and drums throughout. All guitars were recorded by Erlandsson at EMS except on “Ossarium,” and the closing track, “A Light Radiates Into Tomorrow,” was originally commissioned by Fylkingen. Photography for the release is by Aron Mattsson, with sleeve design by Stephen O’Malley. The tracklist for “Echoes of Impermanence” runs: A Shadow Cast Echoes of Impermanence Ossarium To Fade Away Draped Urn A Light Radiates Into Tomorrow A Shadow Cast by David Granström About David Granström David Granström is a composer and musician from Umeå, in the north of Sweden, a city with a stronghold of extreme musical expression. He grew up playing guitar in a metal band and began composing within that context, work that evolved into solo projects once he gained access to studio facilities next to his rehearsal space. Granström found his own musical voice in electroacoustic composition, applying his programming background to build sound and form governed by algorithmic processes, resulting in music defined by harmonic simplicity paired with spatiotextural complexity, mixing synthetic and acoustic sources with strict digital synthesis techniques. He released his debut album, “Ephemeris,” on XKatedral in October 2016, followed by “A Distant Color, Secluded” on the same label in November 2019, an edition of 300 built from four interrelated pieces. “Empty Room,” recorded between 2019 and 2020, followed on the Hallow Ground label in 2021. Granström also appears on “XKatedral Anthology Series III,” the label’s double-vinyl tenth-anniversary compilation released in May 2026 alongside label figures including Kali Malone, Maria W Horn, Jessica Ekomane and Stephen O’Malley. “Echoes of Impermanence,” out November 6, continues that run and adds the electric guitar to his compositional language for the first time.
items._cn_summary: 瑞典作曲家David Granström即将在XKatedral厂牌发行第四张全长专辑《Echoes of Impermanence》，首支单曲《A Shadow Cast》先行释出。专辑延续了他此前建立在长时长数字合成之上的极简主义电子声学创作路径，同时首次引入电吉他元素，使原本隐于表层之下的riff驱动性格得以浮现。录制工作于Elektronmusikstudion EMS及其个人工作室完成，长期合作伙伴Maria W Horn在标题曲中担任Hurdy-Gurdy演奏，Stephen O'Malley负责唱片设计。Granström的创作语言源自其编程背景，将算法过程与和声简朴、时空织体繁复的听感结合，混融合成与声学音源。新作与Kali Malone、Jessica Ekomane等XKatedral核心人物同属厂牌系列，体现了北欧实验音乐圈层内部的紧密协作。

items.album: SIERRA VEINS interview: ‘Safe enough to let go of some of that control’
items.excerpt: There is a productive contradiction at the centre of SIERRA VEINS: what can appear almost uncontrolled onstage depends on an unusually rigorous degree of preparation.
