items.body: There is a productive contradiction at the centre of SIERRA VEINS: what can appear almost uncontrolled onstage depends on an unusually rigorous degree of preparation. Lighting cues and instrumental parts are fixed in advance, yet the security of that technical structure is precisely what allows the performance to become less predictable, more physical and more responsive to the room. The same relationship between control and surrender exists in the writing process. Images, colours, places and even titles can precede the music itself, so the visual world is not something designed afterwards to illustrate finished songs; it belongs to the same compositional vocabulary from the beginning. That interconnected thinking became particularly explicit on “In The Name Of Blood”, SIERRA VEINS’ second album, released in November 2025. Its exploration of identity, inheritance and DNA coincided with the transition from SIERRA to SIERRA VEINS, while the recurring image of veins and cables allows biology and technology to occupy the same visual language. The album also reflects how profoundly performing has altered the way SIERRA composes: although the stage is not allowed to dictate the writing, certain moments were deliberately created with physical performance in mind. That tension between human instability and machine precision extends well beyond the album. In February 2026, SIERRA VEINS released the 19-track “HypnoVizion 031: SIERRA VEINS” DJ mix, using selection and sequencing to expose musical interests that extend outside her own production, while January 2027 will bring her first Australian dates alongside Carpenter Brut, revisiting an artistic relationship that previously produced “Power”. I spoke with SIERRA VEINS just a while before her performance at Nocuturnal Culture Night Festival in Deutzen – about why artistic abandon requires technical security, composing simultaneously through sound and images, allowing the body to influence electronic music, the changing meaning of songs once they reach the stage, collaboration as a question of shared emotional language, and why the next significant evolution of SIERRA VEINS may happen visually before it happens musically. In The Name Of Blood by SIERRA VEINS Sierra Veins interview Karo: I have seen you live several times now, and one thing that keeps fascinating me is that I never feel I am watching exactly the same show twice. The visual language is recognisable, the songs are familiar, but the physical intensity, the movement and even the way the light seems to interact with you change every time. How much of a SIERRA VEINS performance is actually fixed, and how much is allowed to mutate according to the room, the audience and your own state that night? Is there a carefully constructed structure that gives you the freedom to become almost wild inside it? SIERRA VEINS: I’m glad to hear that. My live show is very structured: the lighting and the parts I play with my instruments are predetermined in advance, but there are many things that can vary from one show to another, beyond simply the selection of songs, and make the experience different. The size of the venue, the location or type of festival, the lighting and sound setup, which can change from one place to another, and of course my own performance all have an influence. From one night to another, depending on how I feel and what is happening in the moment, I can interpret a song in one way or another. Karo: You have said that when you begin an album, you often start with atmosphere, images and mood boards before the actual composition, and that with “In The Name Of Blood” the visual world of blood, veins, cables and green existed very early in the process. That makes me wonder whether “visuals” is even the right word, because it suggests something added to music afterwards. Do you experience light, colour, sound and movement as separate elements at all, or are you effectively composing one work in several sensory languages? SIERRA VEINS: Indeed, all the EPs and albums I’ve released so far were written with a universe already in my mind. I often have images, colours, places or even song and album titles in mind before I actually start writing them. Bringing all these ideas together allows me to create a kind of starting point that then guides the way I compose and gives a direction to the whole project. So I don’t really separate the music from everything that surrounds it. For me, it’s all part of the same universe and everything develops together. Karo: There is a contradiction in your stage presence that I find particularly interesting. From the audience it can look uncontrolled, extremely physical, almost feral, yet you have said that when the organisation is precise, the equipment works and everything around the performance is properly under control, your performance becomes much stronger. Does abandon actually require discipline? Do you need to construct a completely safe technical framework before you can allow yourself to become unsafe artistically? SIERRA VEINS: That’s exactly it. When I feel confident and reassured by the technical side of things, and when I feel that the situation is under control, that’s when I can completely let go and feel much freer on stage. I think it’s the same with my writing process. The moments when I manage to go where I really want to go creatively are the moments when I feel safe enough to let go of some of that control. Karo: You have also explained that you thought much more about live performance while writing “In The Name Of Blood”, particularly creating room to move away from the machines and towards the audience. That is interesting because it reverses the usual process of making a record and then figuring out how to perform it. Has the body now entered your compositional thinking from the beginning? When you write something new, do you already know what you will physically need to do with it onstage? SIERRA VEINS: When I started SIERRA VEINS, I didn’t actually intend to perform live. I wrote my first EPs without thinking about any of this, and I was very far from those considerations. Then, little by little, as I started playing more shows, I realised that some tracks that work well on record don’t necessarily translate as well on stage. And the opposite is also true: some tracks that have a strong impact live aren’t necessarily the most listened to. Today, I don’t want those considerations to be at the centre of my mind when I’m writing, but I do like to keep a few ideas about the live show in the back of my mind while I compose. On my latest album, there are definitely some moments that I wrote specifically with the stage in mind. But it’s still very difficult to know in advance how a track will translate live. You only really discover that once you start performing it and seeing how it feels on stage and how the audience responds to it. Karo: The current stage design uses cables as part of the language of veins, blood and identity, but I also read those cables in another way: they belong equally to electronic machinery. The image is simultaneously biological and technological. Is that ambiguity interesting to you? Your music is created electronically, but your performance is intensely bodily; do you see SIERRA VEINS as existing somewhere in that tension between machine precision and the instability of a human body? SIERRA VEINS: Yes, that ambiguity is definitely something that interests me. I’m fascinated by digital art, technology, computer-based music and all of that, but at the same time, it’s very important to me that human emotions remain at the centre of what I write. It’s quite similar on stage. I wouldn’t want to spend an entire 1h10 show behind my machines. I like the idea that my live shows alternate between moments that are purely electronic, where I’m interacting with my machines, and other moments that are more stripped back technologically, with more space for my voice and my physical presence on stage. That contrast between the human and the machine is important to me. Karo: You once said that it is difficult to generalise about audiences from one country to another because the energy can change completely from one concert to the next. Having watched you more than once, that makes sense to me because your performance seems unusually responsive to the immediate space. What actually changes you most: the size of the stage, proximity of the audience, the architecture of the venue, technical limitations, or simply the energy coming back at you? Have you ever walked onstage with one idea of what the concert would be and realised within the first few minutes that the room required something completely different? SIERRA VEINS: I would say the technical aspect is probably what can influence my performance the most. My show is quite demanding technically, both in terms of lighting and sound. And as I mentioned earlier, if I don’t feel confident for one reason or another, my performance on stage will definitely be affected. My energy and mental space might be entirely focused on making sure that everything runs properly from a technical point of view. Then I would say that what can vary the most is the energy coming from the audience. And that really depends on the configuration and size of the venue, the time of the show, etc. There are no rules. But one thing is certain: the more responsive the audience is, the more energy I give on stage. And yes, it happens very often that I walk on stage and, after a few songs, realise that it’s not at all what I expected. You can never really know in advance. Karo: “In The Name Of Blood” deals with identity, inheritance, DNA and the uncomfortable question of how much of ourselves is chosen and how much is already carried within us; even the transition from SIERRA to SIERRA VEINS became part of that idea. But then you have spent months performing those questions repeatedly in front of strangers. Has the live cycle changed your own relationship with the album’s subject? I wonder whether performing a work about identity night after night makes that identity feel more settled, or whether repetition reveals that it is actually much less stable than you thought. SIERRA VEINS: Performing the album on stage for the past few months hasn’t really changed the way I see the questions around identity that I explore on the album. However, my relationship with the songs can change a lot through performing them. Some of them take on a different dimension on stage, and some that I may have felt less attached to at first become very important in the live show, and vice versa. So I would say that it’s not necessarily my perception of my own identity that evolves through performing, but rather my relationship with certain songs. Karo: Your most recent release is “HypnoVizion 031: SIERRA VEINS”, a 19-track DJ mix for HypnoVizion. I find that format interesting in relation to your own records because an album constructs identity through sounds you create, whereas a DJ mix can construct identity through choices, transitions and relationships between other people’s music. What can you say about yourself through selection that you perhaps cannot say through composition? Do you consider sequencing and juxtaposition another form of authorship? SIERRA VEINS: I think DJ mixes are mostly a way for me to show a broader range of my musical tastes. I listen to a lot of music that is quite different from what I produce myself, so it’s a good opportunity to share that side of what I like. There is obviously a creative process in selecting tracks, finding the right transitions and building a progression throughout a mix, so yes, I think it can be a form of authorship, but it’s really difficult to compare it to composing music. Karo: Collaboration has appeared repeatedly in your work, from HEALTH, Carpenter Brut and Gunship around “A Story Of Anger” to Ghost Dance on “Memory Cells” from “In The Name Of Blood”. What makes a collaboration genuinely worthwhile to you? Is the most interesting collaborator someone who understands your language immediately, or someone who introduces an element that initially feels incompatible with it? In other words, are you looking for recognition or productive friction? SIERRA VEINS: A collaboration is really worthwhile when you feel there is an artistic understanding. For me, the most interesting collaborator is someone who speaks the same artistic language, and I don’t necessarily mean having the same artistic universe. I mean someone who understands the emotion, the vibe, even if our universes can sometimes be very different. For me, a good collaboration is mostly about communication and understanding each other from the start. Karo: You have now announced your first Australian tour for 2027 supporting Carpenter Brut, which gives another chapter to a creative relationship that already includes “Power”. Does returning to the same artistic relationship years later feel different once both artists have moved forward? And does touring together create possibilities that a studio collaboration does not, perhaps even for something new to emerge between the projects? SIERRA VEINS: A lot has changed since we first worked on “Power”. The last time we toured together, I hadn’t released an album yet and I had much less experience on stage. So going to Australia together several years later will obviously be a very different experience, and I’m really looking forward to it. As for new collaborations, I’d be very happy to work together again. We’ll see what happens! Karo: You said earlier this year that you were still composing, experimenting with new sounds and working on remixes, but that you deliberately did not want to rush into defining the next release; interestingly, you have also said that although you do not yet know what form that next release will take, you already know something about its visual direction, its colours and its vocabulary. So perhaps this is the right place to finish: when you imagine the next version of SIERRA VEINS, what feels as though it actually needs to change? Is the next step primarily musical, visual, performative, collaborative, or are you beginning to imagine a form in which those distinctions no longer make much sense? SIERRA VEINS: I’m taking a lot of time to experiment with different things, think, and figure out where I want to go next. It’s still a little unclear, but I’m moving forward with my research. Maybe my answer will be different in a few months, but right now, I think the next evolution of the project will probably be more on the visual and graphic side. I won’t say more for now. About SIERRA VEINS SIERRA VEINS is a Paris-based French electronic artist whose work moves through darkwave, EBM, synthwave, techno and heavier electronic forms. The project began in 2017 under the name SIERRA, after a period devoted to learning electronic production, and developed through releases including “Strange Valley,” “Gone” and the 2023 full-length “A Story Of Anger.” The change from SIERRA to SIERRA VEINS was announced in 2025; rather than signalling a musical reinvention, the new name gave a more individual identity to the project and coincided naturally with the themes of inheritance, blood and identity explored on the second album. Released on 7 November 2025, “In The Name Of Blood” centres on identity and the inherited information carried through DNA, with the name change itself incorporated into the album’s creative framework. The record includes “Memory Cells,” created with Ghost Dance, while earlier work has connected SIERRA VEINS with artists including Carpenter Brut, HEALTH and Gunship. Her catalogue has increasingly developed in parallel with an elaborate performance language in which lighting, electronic machinery, voice and movement are conceived as interconnected rather than supplementary elements. That approach is particularly visible in the current “In The Name Of Blood” show, where the visual vocabulary of veins and cables deliberately collapses the distinction between the biological and technological body. In February 2026 she released the 19-track, 46-minute “HypnoVizion 031: SIERRA VEINS” DJ mix, combining her own music with selections from artists including Boys Noize, Matteo Tura, Corvad, Ghost Dance and others. In January 2027, SIERRA VEINS will travel to Australia with Carpenter Brut, joining the project for shows in Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne before both appear at Froth & Fury Festival in Adelaide. The dates extend a collaboration that previously resulted in “Power” and arrive at a point when SIERRA VEINS is deliberately resisting the pressure to define her next release too quickly. For the moment, she suggests that the next substantial transformation may take place first in the project’s visual and graphic language rather than through an immediately identifiable musical shift.
items._cn_summary: 这张访谈深入探讨了SIERRA VEINS如何在高度结构化的技术框架内释放舞台表演的不可控能量。第二张专辑《In The Name Of Blood》围绕身份、遗传与DNA展开创作，视觉意象（血管与电缆）与音乐从同一创作语汇中同步生长，而非事后附庸。生物与科技在统一的视觉语言中交汇，舞台表演经验反向影响了作曲方式，某些段落被明确设计为身体性表演的载体。艺名从SIERRA到SIERRA VEINS的转变标志着艺术身份的深化。专辑延续了人类不稳定性与机器精确性之间的张力，2026年的DJ mix则进一步暴露了艺术家超出自身制作之外的多元音乐趣味。文章为采访形式前半段，侧重创作理念与表演美学，未深入技术细节或具体曲目的音响分析。

items.body: Siouxsie and the Banshees’ long-out-of-print Downside Up, the expansive collection of B-sides and other non-album recordings first released in 2004, will return this fall in newly remastered five-LP and three-CD editions. Due Nov. 20, the revised box set brings together 51 tracks — 49 studio recordings and two live performances — covering material originally issued between 1978 and 1995, from “Voices (On the Air),” the flip side of the band’s debut single “Hong Kong Garden,” through late-period cuts “B Side Ourselves,” “Hang Me High” and “Black Sun.” Along the way, Downside Up collects some of the Banshees’ finest work outside their studio albums, including “Pulled to Bits,” “Drop Dead/Celebration,” “Eve White/Eve Black,” “Red Over White,” “Tattoo,” “Umbrella,” “Something Blue,” “El Día de los Muertos,” “Return” and “Sea of Light.” The set also features the band’s versions of T. Rex’s “20th Century Boy,” Ben E. King’s “Supernatural Thing” and the Modern Lovers’ “She Cracked.” Both configurations have been remastered from the original tapes. The five-LP edition, which marks the collection’s vinyl debut, was cut to lacquer by Miles Showell at Abbey Road Studios and comes with a 32-page booklet featuring new imagery drawn from the Banshees’ original single sleeves. The three-CD clamshell box includes a 68-page booklet. Pre-orders for both editions are now available. Tracklist: LP1 Side 1 Voices (On The Air) 20th Century Boy Pulled To Bits Mittageisen (Metal Postcard) Drop Dead / Celebration Eve White / Eve Black Side 2 Red Over White Follow The Sun Slap Dash Snap Supernatural Thing Congo Conga Coal Mind LP2 Side 3 We Fall Cannibal Roses Obsession II A Sleeping Rain Il Est Né, Le Divin Enfant Tattoo Side 4 (There’s A) Planet In My Kitchen Let Go The Humming Wires I Promise Throw Them To The Lions LP3 Side 5 An Execution The Quarterdrawing Of The Dog Lullaby Umbrella Shooting Sun Side 6 Sleepwalking (On The High Wire) She Cracked She’s Cuckoo Something Blue The Whole Price Of Blood LP4 Side 7 Mechanical Eyes False Face Catwalk Something Wicked (This Way Comes) Are You Still Dying, Darling? Side 8 El Dia De Los Muertos Sunless Staring Back Return Spiral Twist LP5 Side 9 Sea Of Light I Could Be Again Hothead B Side Ourselves Swimming Horses (Live) Side 10 All Tomorrow’s Parties (Live) Hang Me High Black Sun The original four-CD edition contained 55 tracks. The new reissue carries over its first three discs in full: 49 studio recordings plus two performances taped at KROQ’s 1991 Acoustic Christmas, “Swimming Horses” and the Velvet Underground’s “All Tomorrow’s Parties.” The only material omitted is the original box’s fourth disc, which contained the four orchestral rerecordings from the Banshees’ 1984 The Thorn EP: “Overground,” “Voices (On the Air),” “Placebo Effect” and “Red Over White.” The earlier B-side versions of “Voices (On the Air)” and “Red Over White” remain in the new collection. Box-set preorders placed through the official Siouxsie and the Banshees webshop will include an exclusive print hand-signed by Siouxsie while supplies last. The print will accompany the first 500 five-LP box-set orders and the first 300 three-CD box-set orders. For U.S. fans, a new Siouxsie and the Banshees shop will launch Friday, Sept. 11, at 11 a.m. EDT, allowing customers to order with domestic postage. A separate allocation of box sets accompanied by the signed print has been reserved for the U.S. store. The shop link will be available through the band’s official Linktree. items._cn_summary: 该合集汇集了Siouxsie and the Banshees乐队1978至1995年间的B面及非专辑录音，共51首，包含49首录音室作品和两首1991年KROQ现场演出。作为B面合集，它展示了乐队在专辑正篇之外更为自由的面貌，涵盖从早期翻唱T. Rex的《20th Century Boy》到后期曲目，并收录了《Pulled to Bits》《Tattoo》《Sea of Light》等代表作品。新版本经原磁带重新母带，首次发行五黑胶与三CD两种配置，并附有全新册子，由Abbey Road工作室刻盘。这些曲目在哥特暗潮基调上融入了实验性声音处理与多样风格尝试，是追溯乐队创作全貌的重要补充。

items._cn_summary: 这是Orquesta Akokán的第四张专辑，延续了对经典古巴声音的忠实再现，以大型乐队编制呈现充满生气的节奏律动。开篇曲在歌声与乐队演奏之间逐步升温，结尾的Afro-Cuban Mambo加入华丽女声，使整体在庄重与欢快之间取得平衡。乐评强调其现代制作手法与复古古巴风格并存，既保留了非洲-古巴音乐传统的韵律光泽，又带有当代拉丁音乐的可听性。这种兼具历史厚度和现场感染力的处理方式，也是Daptone厂牌对其青睐的原因。专辑中的铜管组、打击乐与人声层次分明，适合从传统拉丁节奏切入世界音乐聆听体验的听众。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It truly feels otherworldly, a blend of metal guitar, progressive rock, and chamber music, alongside something that defies words and enters (fortunately) an ethereal musical realm. The lineup chosen by Ian Alexander, a guitarist born in Cologne, Germany, features two drummers, a vibraphonist, and a harpist. This lends a unique, personal atmosphere to the album; while Alexander has always sought to express his deepest passions in his solo work, here they manifest in a distinctive way. On tracks like "Tau Librae," the guitar sounds heavily distorted at times, yet by the time we reach "Electric Water Experience," the arpeggios take flight, evoking pure fusi�n, albeit of an experimental nature that feels both familiar and strange. It is like those sci-fi movies where someone we know is replaced by a body double that looks exactly the same... yet something feels "off." In this case, however, there is no jarring noise, only excellent, highly dynamic, and hypnotic music. Alexander found the perfect vehicle and the right "bodywork" to convey the emotions he intended, even when they might seem contradictory; ultimately, because they spring from the same soul, they do not conflict, but rather make as much sense as melody and harmony themselves.Clairvoyance resonates with echoes and hints of space rock; the harp and drums form an ideal pairing, balanced by a guitar that, at will, introduces calm, stillness, and repose. Alexander explores various styles throughout the album; the sound can evoke vast open plains one moment, yet feel claustrophobic the next, like climbing an endless spiral staircase in an early 20th-century novel. At times, the music turns powerful and almost funk-like, then scales upward, building tension through the magic of electric guitar textures, later joined by the vibraphone. Each track is unique; on "Attack of the Android Jester," Alexander plays bass, delivering an infectious groove that suddenly shifts into strange frequencies mimicking electronic sounds, all while a beautiful progressive passage gradually takes shape. Jazz-rock fusion resurfaces, as it does whenever Tau Librae performs, with compositions so accomplished they speak to Alexander's maturity as both a songwriter and a performer."Mothership" begins with an almost electronic feel, underpinned by a jazzy drum foundation reminiscent of Weather Report; the dual-drummer setup is noticeable, and a certain dissonance contributes to an eerie atmosphere that never actually undermines the melody.The classic harp format is utilized at the start of "Windowpane / Courage and Corrosion", evoking a different sense of time, a moment of carving out a space and dwelling there. Those produced echoes linger longer, like a stone skillfully skipped across a lake. Eastern tradition meets Western as the track enters its second section, a modern epic, if such a term applies, representing the new language Alexander sought, and suddenly the album's title, "The Nineteenth Star of the Libra Constellation," takes on a new meaning, reflecting that drive to pull us from our comfort zone and transport us to somewhere entirely new.
items._genre: jazz-rock fusion / experimental progressive / chamber music
items._cn_summary: 德国科隆吉他手Ian Alexander的专辑以两位鼓手、颤音铁琴与竖琴的特殊编制为核心，将金属吉他失真、前卫摇滚与室内乐质感融于一体。乐评指出，作品在'Tau Librae'中呈现沉重失真，到'Electric Water Experience'转入纯融合琶音，风格流转间营造出既熟悉又陌生的氛围，类似科幻电影中被替换的'替身'——表面上无可挑剔，深处却暗藏异样情绪。竖琴与鼓的对话形成开阔而内省的空间感，'Clairvoyance'带出太空摇滚余韵，'Attack of the Android Jester'则以贝斯律动骤然转向电子化频段，后接前卫段落铺展。'Mothership'借双鼓配置与Weather Report式爵士律动构建不安底色，'Windowpane'开篇以经典竖琴语法切入，后段融入东西方传统对话，呈现代史诗感。整体展现出融合多元风格的高度成熟与个人化表达。

items.body: Laibach released “WAT” on 8 September 2003 through Mute Records. The album turns 23 this year. Iztok Turk and Laibach produced the record, with Umek co-producing and sharing mixing duties with Turk; Nilesh Patel handled mastering at The Exchange. The track “Anti-Semitism” was separately produced and mixed by Temponauta. “WAT” is an acronym for “We Are Time,” revealed on the title track. Laibach has described the album’s intent as being not about “what Laibach is, or what it wants, but what you are and where you stand.” What is on Laibach’s ‘WAT’ The CD edition runs 12 tracks: “B Mashina”, “Tanz mit Laibach”, “Du bist unser”, “Achtung!”, “Ende”, “Now You Will Pay”, “Hell: Symmetry”, “Das Spiel ist aus”, “Satanic Versus”, “The Great Divide”, “WAT” and “Anti-Semitism”, with a total running time of 58:23. The 2LP vinyl edition replaces “Now You Will Pay” in its track sequence with the bonus cut “Reject or Breed” and runs 62:27. The CD also carries an enhanced video for “Tanz mit Laibach”. Tomi Meglič of Siddharta contributed music, lyrics and additional vocals on “B Mashina”. Long-time NSK collaborator Peter Mlakar wrote lyrics for “Du bist unser” and “Achtung!”. Slavko Avsenik Jr. arranged the choir parts and co-wrote the title track, and Matej Mršnik played guitar on “Ende”. “Tanz mit Laibach” was released as a single on 25 August 2003, with remixes by Umek, Johannes Heil, Zeta Reticula and Temponauta, and an accompanying video directed by Sašo Podgoršek. About Laibach Laibach formed in 1980 in Trbovlje, a mining town in Slovenia, then part of Yugoslavia. The band’s name is the German-language name for Ljubljana, a deliberate reference to the World War II occupation of Slovenia. In December 1984, Laibach co-founded Neue Slowenische Kunst (NSK) alongside the visual-art collective Irwin and the Scipion Nasice Sisters Theatre, uniting music, art and theatre under a single project. The band released its debut album, “Laibach”, in 1985 through the Slovenian label ŠKUC Ropot. From 1987 onward, Laibach recorded primarily for Mute Records, releasing “Krst pod Triglavom – Baptism” and “Opus Dei” in 1987, followed by covers albums “Let It Be” (1988) and “Sympathy for the Devil” (1988/1990). “Kapital” followed in 1992, then “NATO” in 1994, reworking military and pop songs against the backdrop of the Yugoslav wars, and “Jesus Christ Superstars” in 1996, a reinterpretation of the Andrew Lloyd Webber rock opera. “WAT” arrived in 2003, continuing the band’s practice of operating as a collective rather than a fixed lineup. Laibach followed “WAT” with the career-spanning compilation “Anthems” in 2004 and the national-anthem reworking “Volk” in 2006. The band has continued releasing new material into the 2020s, including the symphonic work “Alamut” in 2025 and the studio album “Musick” in 2026.
items._cn_summary: 《WAT》是斯洛文尼亚乐队Laibach于2003年发行的专辑，作为“我们即时间”的缩写，专辑延续了乐队作为集体而非固定阵容的创作模式。曲目涵盖工业电子、舞曲节奏与合唱编排，标题曲由合唱团合作呈现，并由Siddharta成员参与其中一首词曲创作。专辑通过反战、宗教、极权等议题展开对听者立场的质问，其制作结合了多位混音与母带工程师，包括斯洛文尼亚电子音乐人Umek的参与。歌词以德语与英语交替，融合军事化节奏与仪式感合唱，延续乐队自1980年代以来以视觉与剧场美学介入音乐的传统。该作既是其工业实验脉络的延续，也是对集体身份与历史记忆的又一次声音重构。

items.body: We were looking forward to being able to talk on the podcast this week about the Diavol Strain set we caught on Sunday, however that won’t be the case. After an apparently awful border crossing into the US the Chilean duo understandably opted not to cross into Canada, as doing so would of course necessitate another entry into the US. Us not getting to see the band behind arguably the year’s best goth record thus far is obviously a drop in the ocean in comparison to larger inconveniences, threats, and acts of violence and murder committed by the current US administration, but it’s a reminder that fascism wants to keep people apart, wants to deny us the opportunity to meet with and learn from those from other parts of the world. You don’t need us to say it, but fuck ICE, fuck white supremacy, fuck everything and everyone related to this atrocity of an American government. Divider Kontravoid, “Without” Oh shit, new Kontravoid incoming. One of the hardest working (and at this point most influential) darkwave acts has been on a tear for a couple of years, with successive banger releases that border on harder industrial, pure synthpop and may other sounds. “Without” continues that trend, with Cam Findlay stretching himself vocally in ways we’ve not yet heard on the new cut, especially on the double-time chorus. Anthemic stuff, and a fine harbinger of what’s to come on October 2nd. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Dark Chisme, “Suffer Like Me” Seattle’s darkwave duo Dark Chisme has been building their audience the old-fashioned way: by releasing good music, and kicking rich amounts of ass live every time the roll through town. It’s been a real pleasure to watch first hand, especially on their recent show opening up for Omar Doom here in Vancouver where they tore it up on all their established songs, and also tossed this new one “Suffer Like Me” into the mix, which unsurprisingly went over just as well as any other cut they played. Loving the little hints of NRG and freestyle making their way into their sound here, and very keen to hear them continue in this vein in the lead-up to their next album. Suffer Like Me by Dark Chisme Synapscape, “Melting” We’ve had a lot of fun tracking Philipp Münch as he’s dodged down ever odder alleyways over the last few years, from wilfully naive synthpop to oddball dark electro, but a reconvening with Tim Kniep for the project which first brought him international attention is always welcome. Plenty of familiar core elements from across Synapscape’s legacy of powernoise jump out on this teaser from The Future, but the polyrhythmic density which builds up and spirals outward beneath Münch’s restless yowl pushes the envelope quite pleasantly. the future by synapscape Divider, “Nought Point Zero (Portion Control Remix)” Divider’s Zero has been one of the most enjoyable EBM releases of the year, showing how much can be wrought from a little bit of structural experimentation while still holding to no-frills and hard-hitting sound design. Sounds a little like modern day PorCon, no? It’s not surprising, then, to hear how easily a Portion Control bassline can be welded to the moonlit junkyard ambience of the original version of this cut from that record. Nought Point Zero by Divider Silent EM, “Survive (Luminance Remix)” Silent EM isn’t exactly striking while the iron’s hot with a remix LP coming out nearly two full years since the release of Real Life, but a list of contributors including Ortrotasce, Inhalt, Qual, Kontravoid, and Un Hombre Solo brings a lot of star power to this better late than never comp. In particular, the mix of dreamy ghostliness and precise electro pulses on this mix from Brussels-based Luminance is what’s really jumping off the page at us. Silent EM – Real Life (Remixes) by No. Nothing. Never. Records SØLVE, “Nothing Lasts” As is tradition, Brant Showers has released a song on his Birthday as a pay what you want single on Bandcamp. In this case, the song in question is a cover of Matthew Sweet’s “Nothing Lasts”, a classic bit of pop-rock melancholia from the beloved by those who know Girlfriend LP. Far from taking the song into the territory of his usual post-witchhouse ritual dark ambience, Showers plays it straight, amping the spare original into a shoegazey alsice of orchestral pop. Unexpected and absolutely lovely. NOTHING LASTS by SØLVE The post Tracks: September 8th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: There is something almost indecent about hearing Soft Cell look backward with this much grace. For a band that once made sleaze, synthetic dread, cheap rooms, lust, humiliation, and metropolitan bad behaviour feel like the natural furniture of pop music, The Rainbow Room finds Marc Almond and Dave Ball staring across Manhattan from 65 floors up and realizing that memory can be every bit as dangerous as desire. The song comes from Danceteria, Soft Cell’s sixth and final studio album, completed shortly before Ball’s death in October 2025. It’s set in New York in the early ’80s, when Almond and Ball were recording at Mediasound, running around clubs, meeting Warhol, dancing near Madonna, and absorbing a city seemingly built for people with nowhere respectable to be. The Rainbow Room catches that romance at the point where exhilaration develops a crack. Ball’s arrangement is spacious, elegant, and slightly narcotic. The electronics drift rather than stampede, giving Almond room to sing as though he were paging through photographs nobody else can see. His voice carries wisdom and gravitas; every phrase has the peculiar steadiness of a man who knows how unreliable memory can be yet still chooses to trust it – albeit with rose coloured glasses. This is, in short, Almond’s My Way. The central image comes from Almond’s own birthday visit to Rockefeller Center. “… I did celebrate my birthday – my 21st or 22nd – at The Rainbow Room in the Rockefeller Center… The story of that view is true, too, I really did think: “Imagine falling down there” at the time,” Almond muses. “It was important to mention the Twin Towers, to acknowledge that this song about the future had a poignancy to it, knowing how dark that future would become.” That line about falling is pure Soft Cell: glamour sharing a table with dread, champagne beside the abyss. The Twin Towers turn the song’s future tense into something brutal. Young Almond looks across New York wondering what comes next; older Almond sings from a world in which several answers are already known, including the death of his musical partner. That knowledge changes the record’s emotional gravity. Ball heard the finished album before he passed away, and Almond has said no further Soft Cell recordings are possible without him. The Rainbow Room therefore carries a strange double exposure of youth and aftermath: two men in New York discovering possibility, then those same lives heard decades later through distance, death, and accumulated history. The Rainbow Room takes nostalgia somewhere quieter and more devastating. The city still glitters below, the party is still downstairs, and Almond stands at the window remembering when the future looked endless. Listen below: With the untimely death of Dave Ball in 2025, the band’s sixth and final album, Danceteria, finally arrives on September 25, 2026. You can pre-order Danceteria here. Marc Almond has announced another live run, this time in South America in late November to December. Prior to that, Marc will be playing more European shows in Italy and Poland from late September to October. In early November, Marc returns to the States for a second time this year and will be touring as Soft Cell. The tour begins November 8th in San Diego and includes the Darker Waves festival in California on November 14th. Check out the full listings and ticket links here. Nov 8 San Diego, CA – The Magnolia Nov 10 Napa, CA – Uptown Theatre Nov 11 San Francisco, CA – The Regency Ballroom Nov 13 Reno, NV – Grand Sierra Resort/Casino Nov 14 Huntington Beach, CA – Darker Waves Nov 15 San Luis Obispo, CA – Fremont Theater Follow Soft Cell: Website Instagram Facebook Spotify The post Soft Cell Shares Moving Synthpop Ballad “The Rainbow Room” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦Soft Cell最后一支单曲《The Rainbow Room》，出自乐队第六张也是最终的录音室专辑《Danceteria》，在Dave Ball于2025年10月去世后于2026年9月发行。歌曲以Almond早年在纽约Rockefeller Center庆祝生日的真实经历为蓝本，描绘他从65层高空俯瞰曼哈顿时对未来的遐想与对坠落深渊的恐惧。Ball的编曲开阔、优雅且带有轻度麻醉感，电子音色漂浮而非冲击，为Almond的声线留出空间，使其呈现出历经岁月后的沉稳与智慧。乐评特别强调作品中帝国大厦与世贸双子塔意象所承载的预言式悲怆——青年Almond的凝视在数十年后因Ball离世、世贸遭袭而被赋予了沉重含义。整首歌将青春的迷醉与暮年的追忆叠合于同一段旋律，使怀旧情绪走向更为安静而深沉的维度。

items.body:
Steven Bernstein: The Busiest Man in Show Biz

by Troy Collins


Steven Bernstein © 2026 Andrew Blackstein




A key presence on the New York scene over the past 30 years, trumpeter, composer, arranger, and bandleader Steven Bernstein has immersed himself in such a wide array of music with his bands Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Diaspora Soul, Universal Melody Brass Band, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and the Butler-Bernstein Hot 9 that his output defies easy categorization. A former member of The Lounge Lizards and Levon Helm’s Midnight Ramble Band, Bernstein has also composed works for film, theater, and dance in addition to doing arrangements for a diverse list of artists, including Lou Reed, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Allen Toussaint, Marianne Faithfull, Linda Ronstadt, Rufus Wainwright, Darlene Love, Mario Pavone, Bill Frisell, and John Lurie. His lengthy list of sideman credits includes appearances on recent recordings by Laurie Anderson (Heart of a Dog), Roswell Rudd (Trombone for Lovers), Mostly Other People Do the Killing (Loafer’s Hollow), Antony and the Johnsons (Turning), and Nels Cline (Lovers). He also continues to perform with Ray Anderson’s Pocket Brass Band, Omaha Diner, and the Kamikaze Ground Crew.

Born in Berkeley, California, Bernstein moved to New York in 1978. By 1990 he had joined The Lounge Lizards, appearing on the group’s 1991 release Live in Berlin (Intuition). Shortly before that, in 1988 he formed the trio Spanish Fly with slide guitarist Dave Tronzo and tuba virtuoso Marcus Rojas. By 1995, producer Hal Willner, a fan of Spanish Fly, enlisted Bernstein as arranger for the soundtrack to Robert Altman’s film Kansas City, which led to collaborations on numerous other Willner projects, including tributes to Bill Withers, Doc Pomus, and Leonard Cohen, among many others.

In 1996, Bernstein formed Sexmob with saxophonist Briggan Krauss, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Kenny Wollesen. It remains his primary vehicle for exploring the slide trumpet, a rare instrument that he picked up in a Woodstock guitar shop back in 1977. Over two decades of recording, the group has put their singular stamp on an eclectic list of tunes by the likes of Leadbelly, John Barry, Hoagy Carmichael, Paul McCartney, Duke Ellington, Prince, Kurt Cobain, the Rolling Stones, James Brown, Count Basie, Professor Longhair, and Nino Rota. The group’s latest album, in its 20th anniversary year, is Cultural Capital, the first Sexmob recording to feature all original compositions.

From 1999 to 2008, Bernstein contributed four recordings to John Zorn’s Radical Jewish Culture series on his Tzadik label – 1999’s Diaspora Soul (featuring members of The Lounge Lizards and Sexmob), 2002’s Diaspora Blues (featuring Sam Rivers), 2004’s Diaspora Hollywood (inspired by classic film composers and West Coast cool jazz), and 2008’s Diaspora Suite (a homecoming recorded with Bay Area musicians). Each project combined traditional cantorial songs and elements of jazz, blues, and rock.

Bernstein’s Millennial Territory Orchestra debuted with 2006’s MTO, Vol. 1, which featured large ensemble interpretations of songs by Stevie Wonder, Prince, and the Grateful Dead, as well as Benny Moten and Charlie Johnson and His Paradise Band. They followed with 2008’s We Are MTO, which included renditions of tunes by Fats Waller, Don Redman, Count Basie, and the Beatles. Their 2011 recording, MTO Plays Sly, was a tribute to the music of Sly & The Family Stone and featured the late P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell along with guest vocalists.

In 2012, Bernstein joined up with New Orleans piano master Henry Butler in the retro-flavored Butler, Bernstein and the Hot 9. Their critically acclaimed 2014 Impulse! debut, Viper’s Drag, featured spirited renditions of Fats Waller’s title track along with tunes by Jelly Roll Morton and originals by Butler. The restlessly creative Bernstein continues to juggle several working bands. During a recent residency at The Stone in NYC, he performed with Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, Spanish Fly, Blue Campfire, and Universal Melody Brass Band.

Bernstein’s latest album is ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance (Royal Potato Family). In the liner notes, Bernstein mentions being enchanted by Burning Spear’s Garvey’s Ghost (Island, 1976) back in 1981, only realizing years later that it was a dub version of Marcus Garvey, Burning Spear’s Island release from the previous year. Since then, Bernstein has wanted to record an acoustic jazz trio album and have the results remade as a dub album. The first half of the release, ResoNation Trio, features Bernstein on trumpets, Scott Colley on contrabass, and Nasheet Waits on drums. To challenge himself, Bernstein eschews his main axe (slide trumpet) for this session and instead plays regular valve trumpet, G trumpet, and flugelhorn. The second half is called Ultra Resonance and features the first session tapes remixed and rearranged in dub fashion by longtime producer Scotty Hard, who also adds various keyboards, samples, and percussion to the mix. The former date is as spartan as the latter is dense, yet the two recordings (different though they are in concept and execution), are inextricably linked. I interviewed Bernstein in the summer of 2026, shortly after the release of ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance.

 

* * *

 

Troy Collins: You’ve been touring with Laurie Anderson the past few years, as documented by the recently released Let X = X (Nonesuch), which features Sexmob as Anderson’s backing band. What has it been like interpreting and rearranging her tunes for Sexmob, especially since Sexmob (in)famously doesn’t typically use pre-arranged tunes and/or setlists? And perhaps more importantly, how did this particular collaboration come about and what is working with Anderson herself like?

Steven Bernstein: Playing with Laurie has been a life-changing experience. She is completely about creation, being in the moment, acting on every inspiration, trying every idea and having fun. Her work ethic is legendary. Her ability to transform an audience is mastery. So being around her and that energy is just a powerful and positive situation. Even though a “show” is basically set once Laurie has decided on it (we are touring a completely different concert, different songs, different stories, different visuals, and a different “theme”) we/she are constantly making changes. Every show day we are at the theatre by 2:00 pm (she gets there at 11:00 am to start working with the lighting director) and we run every piece, whether a new idea comes from Laurie, me, another member of the band, a random sound that makes Laurie say “What’s that? Let’s try that in ‘___’.” Every idea is entertained and often added to the show.

The story of how this all started is beautiful. I’ve been around Laurie and known her at a distance for a long time, but the first time we really worked closely was doing Hal Willner’s Leonard Cohen show in Brighton in 2004. I arranged two songs for her, “The Guest” and “If It Be Your Will.” At Hal’s memorial she wanted to do Lou Reed’s “Gassed and Stoked.” I brought an arrangement that sounded just like the record and we played it through. She turned to me and said, “that sounds great, but I had another idea, I have this new loop” and she starts activating the loop with her violin bowing. It was a very “Laurie-style” loop: rhythmic, sonic, and not in 4/4 time. Tony and Kenny just drop in and start playing. It was grooving and effortless from the first sound. Laurie ended up testing positive for Covid and was unable to play the memorial, but a week later she calls and says how much fun she had playing with us. She said, “I’ve never had that feeling playing music” and that Warners is re-releasing her records and she was thinking of revisiting her older material (which she had never done), and asked would Sexmob play with her? You know my answer.

TC: Since you mentioned him, I’d be remiss to not ask about your years working with Hal Willner. The man’s various artist projects were significant touchstones in my development as a listener. I know he was a big fan of Spanish Fly – is that how you first met? And how did you become his go-to arranger for so many of his projects?

SB: I heard Hal’s Nino Rota record the summer of 1981 while visiting back home in Berkeley. Peter Engelhart, the legendary metal percussion maker played it for me (his daughters are some of my oldest and best friends). It changed my DNA! After that it became a thing. Who is Hal Willner? Where is Hal Willner? I did Night Music with Karen Mantler in 1989. I also played with Carla Bley, Bootsy, and Allen Toussaint on that show. Hal came up to me and said that he was a fan of Spanish Fly, that he’d been coming to our gigs at the Knitting Factory (lurking in the back I’m sure). He gave me his number and said that he would love to help us in any way he could. That led to him producing the first Spanish Fly record (on Knitting Factory records). It is a great Hal Willner production. Hal and I had very similar musical loves and ideas about music, he believed in me and kept offering me amazing opportunities. That led to a 25-year relationship. He could ask me to arrange for Elton John, Bill Frisell, Nick Cave, Lou Reed, Courtney Love, Robert Altman, Marshall Allan, U2 – it was always magic and natural. When I met him, it was pre-internet, and I would keep a pad of paper next to me during our phone conversations. His references could be Ernie Kovacs, Rahsaan, Allan Ginsberg, Martin Denny, Dorothy Parker, Anne Waldman, The Three Stooges, Gregory Corso, Fellini ... I did my best to keep up and learned a lot.

TC: Talking about Willner reminds me that you’ve done arrangements for more people than I can list, and the stylistic variety of artists is staggering. I’m curious if there’s ever been any job you feel you couldn’t or wouldn’t do?

To clarify, the beautiful thing about music is that someone else can take a song that seems unsalvageable and make something new from it that the original author may not have ever suspected was possible. Having just listened to a recent interview with Bill Frisell, I was reminded of his rendition of Madonna’s “Live To Tell,” which transforms what I would consider to be a lightweight pop song into a rhapsodic epic.

You are obviously capable of the same magic, but I wonder, have there ever been offers that you’ve refused based on the material or direction that someone wanted to go with it? Have you ever encountered a song that you felt was simply unredeemable?

SB: Well, there’s a funny story from about 8 years ago, at the beginning of Trump’s 1st term. It was a slow time (as often is the case for freelance workers) and I got an email from someone about arranging/producing some songs. The guy is a Sexmob fan, knows my work with Hal, and he has written some protest songs, tells me he thinks he can get Bono to sing on them, etc. He is not a professional musician, but this is his passion. He also has a vision of a performance piece situation, where the song is played while the listener goes down the “golden elevator” and walks somewhere else. We agree to a fee and he sends me the demo. He is playing rudimentary chords on the piano, and sings one verse, one chorus – it’s about 25 seconds. I call him and ask if there is more, he says no that’s the song. I explain that songs usually have a second or third verse, maybe a bridge, but he says no this is the song. I explain to him that it’s about 25 seconds, and if he wants it to work the way he is envisioning, (going down the elevator and walking) it needs to be at least 3 minutes long. He says, “Well do that Sexmob thing.” I talk to my wife and tell her that I don’t know if I can do this and she says “I thought you said you can make music out of anything.” So, I did and it ended up very cool!

TC: Well then, the obvious follow-up question to that is – did Bono sing on it?

SB: NO. A total pipe dream!

TC: Since we’ve been talking about arranging, I assume nothing is off limits in your own bands regarding your original tunes. Are there any pieces specifically written for say Sexmob, Millennial Territory Orchestra, or Spanish Fly that don’t translate as well from one band to the other, or do you compose your pieces so that any of your bands can perform them?

SB: Each piece is written not only for the band, but specifically for the players in each band. So, there hasn’t been much crossover. There is a piece I wrote as a commission during the pandemic that I played with Sexmob and MTO, but it really worked better as an MTO piece. But the very last phrase (the kicker) of the MTO end of night theme came from a Spanish Fly composition!

TC: Let’s move on to your new album. Your latest release for Royal Potato Family, ResoNation Trio/Ultra Resonance present two very different facets of your artistry – the former title finds you playing on valve trumpet and flugelhorn (instead of the ubiquitous slide trumpet) accompanied by bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, while the later features Scotty Hard remixing the trio. How did this project come about and when did you first meet and work with Scotty Hard? It seems to me your working relationship with Hard goes all the way back to the very first Sexmob album, 1998’s Din of Inequity.

SB: This project came about because of a grant from the Shifting Foundation. The idea of creating original music with the orchestration of valve trumpet, acoustic bass, and drum set has been a dream of mine for a very long time. This particular vibrational intersection is not widely used, so the unknown possibilities are vast. On a musical/improvisational/technical level it has a very specific set of challenges, and it has taken me this long to feel ready to undertake this long-held desire. Scott Colley and Nasheet were always the musicians I wanted to do this with; I have known them both a long time, and they are veteran masters of spontaneous composition. Another long-held dream has been to create a dub version of an improvisatory instrumental record. I heard Garvey’s Ghost in 1981, and it changed my DNA. Once I started making my own records, I was just waiting for the right opportunity ... and this was it. The trio record is purely conversational and in the moment; back porch music with unlimited harmonic and structural possibilities. The time spent on this record was the decades of playing and writing that preceded it. Ultra Resonance is a mirror image, in that Scott creates his pieces layer by layer, adding and subtracting sounds and rhythms – it takes weeks to build a track.

When I first started playing in The Lounge Lizards with Michael Blake on tenor, Scotty started coming to hang; he was a friend of Michael’s from Vancouver. The first session we did with him was for a Justin Warfield record on Quincy Jones’ label Qwest. It was produced by Prince Paul (I am a huge fan of De La Soul). Scotty wrote the horn chart and engineered. Scotty went on to record and produce the first four Sexmob records. I was already doing fast cuts and dropouts live, but Scotty’s mixes/arrangements shaped the sound of the band.

TC: Having just listened to Sexotica (Thirsty Ear, 2006), your collaborative effort with the production duo known as GoodandEvil (Danny Blume and Chris Castagno), I’m curious how that experience was compared to your similar efforts with Scotty Hard? How does GoodandEvil’s working method differ from Hard’s and what are your thoughts on the different outcomes?

SB: Regarding the two albums/processes – they were fundamentally different as working methods and outcomes. We went into Sexotica (which got a Grammy nomination) with the idea of creating a project that was half acoustic and half electronic. Sexmob went on and recorded all the compositions (two of them being loose jams with input from Danny Blume). Then we did a full day of overdubs with Kenny: wood percussion, metal percussion, bird whistles, and gongs. Then GoodandEvil did their magic. Some pieces skewed more acoustic, some more electronic. The idea was an even balance overall.

With Ultra Resonance Scott was given all the tracks (20 songs). The first track he made, “Titano,” was a piece that’s not on the trio record, but I felt it would be a good piece for Scotty to put his magic on. I figured he would do a “remix” of it, but he rewrote the bass line and created a brand-new piece (natch). After that it was just letting Scott experiment and follow his muse. We had mapped out a series of “zones” we wanted the pieces to be in, but everything Scotty created was totally unexpected. Part of this was the idea of intentional experimentation – on both of our parts. For me it was the idea of the acoustic record, for Scotty it was some new boxes/plug-ins that he had recently received, and the idea of not going back to his tried-and-true techniques. Also, with Sexotica I was not involved in their process, but with Scotty I would hang in the studio once the “track” was created, and was involved in arranging process (Scott claims I had 3 good ideas, I’d say more like 7.6).

As far as my thoughts on the outcomes – two singular recordings that I believe are unlike anything else in the modern recording world. I’m proud of that.

TC: Switching gears slightly (towards acoustic sounds), you’re a fan of vintage horns. I’m assuming that there are certain models you never take on tour and some that you take on the road more frequently? What are the criteria for those distinctions? And what about the slide trumpet? I’m not familiar with anyone else playing one, so where and when did you ever find one?

SB: Vintage trumpets aren’t an issue on the road. I just use the horn best suited for the music. The horn I used touring with Levon Helm was a handmade Chicago Benge from 1947. That was a horn that could project over a five-piece horn section and two electric guitars. It had amazing response and Levon could feel my beat matching his. That’s not what I need with Laurie Anderson!

Regarding the slide trumpet – I found my first horn in a guitar store in Woodstock in 1977 when I was attending Creative Music Studio. When I started Sexmob 30 years ago my old friend (and master repairman) Dick Akright in Oakland (who I met in 6th grade) built the horn I use. It’s one a kind! I’ve collected almost every brand of slide trumpet over the years, though they are not as playable as my horn.

The first horn was $25, at the time (mid-70s) and many trumpet players had one because they were cheap and easily available.

TC: Speaking of Levon Helm, what was it like working with Helm and how did that relationship come about?

SB: This is a long story. I knew Levon had been having “rent party” gigs at the barn. Tony Scherr had done some, and Erik Lawrence did as well. Levon was in danger of losing the barn, as this was a last-ditch attempt to raise some money and also make some music. Erik had invited me to play a few times, and there was a Saturday where I was available (I often did a wedding on Saturday, as I was raising a family, and those gigs paid the bills). Anyway, they mention a few songs Levon might want to do (no Band songs) and said come up early because we might rehearse. We got up there and Levon didn’t come out, so I sat with a boombox and learned a few more songs that Levon “might want to do.” It was a nice chill hang up there, and when it became clear that there was not going to be any rehearsing, I told Erik Lawrence “Don’t play what I play. You just play what you hear, and I’ll play what I hear.” That way we were both free to react to the music. We were playing with Olabelle, and Levon just walked up and got behind the drums. It was the most natural improvisation/spontaneous composition. Levon didn’t know my name, had never seen me before, just smiled at me and told me what he needed with his drum fills. It was magic, and in true Levon form, he put a song from that night on one of his CD’s. Pure improvisation – we had never met!

As far as working with him – it was some of the most magic, swinging, joyous, pure music I have ever had the opportunity to create. He taught me so much about playing in time, playing melody, playing directly from the heart to the people. He was as great and real and no bullshit and smart as you would think from his legendary status. And we had FUN. And he went from almost losing everything to winning three Grammys in eight years!

TC: Speaking of legendary performers, how did you meet pianist Henry Butler, and what was your working relationship with him like?

SB: Another long and beautiful story. In the summer of 1984, I was working with the Flying Karamazov Brothers. We spent two months doing a show at the Goodman Theater in Chicago, and then went on to do a second show at the Olympic Arts Festival in LA. When that was over, they invited me up to the Eugene Country Fair, a legendary hippie festival that was associated with Ken Kesey and the Grateful Dead family. When they asked if I’d like to join them on the Old Time New Age Chataqua tour, a traveling group of “New Vaudevillians” – musicians and environmental activists that toured small communities in the rural Northwest, camping out and putting on shows – that seemed like a better option than returning to my non-air-conditioned fifth story walk up apartment on 109th street in July.

Our first stop was our one actual “gig,” at the Vancouver Folk Festival, and we headed up there directly from the Eugene Country Fair, where we had been enjoying the kind of quality research one would associate with the Grateful Dead Community. As we entered the festival, I heard a sound I was not expecting at a folk festival – a piano player, playing and singing music that seemed like it was completely futuristic, and at the same time playing music that seemed to come from early pre-jazz America. I had never heard anything like this, and at first, I thought my ears and brain were still vibrating from my Country Fair adventures, but it was actually being played, and it was (a pre-Impulse records) Henry Butler. He completely changed my DNA and I became a fan, buying his records when they came out.

When the Kansas City soundtrack record came out on Verve records, it was a time of flowing money in the record business, CDs were selling, and I believe the Bertleman Family had bought the Verve company. In 1995 they organized a cross-country tour with the Joe Henderson Trio, Charlie Haden Quartet West, and the Kansas City All-Stars, which included many Verve artists. I was the musical director of a band that included David “Fathead” Newman, Don Byron, Nicholas Payton, Christian McBride, James Carter, Mark Whitfield, etc.

I had contracted the band but was unable to find a piano player (Gerri Allen and Cyrus Chesnut had done the movie). I contacted seemingly every pianist in NYC who would fit the bill, and none were available, and I was starting to panic. I called Hal Willner to ask his advice and without missing a beat he said “did you call Henry Butler?” And that’s how it all started.

Henry and I were kindred spirits and when the tour was over he told me we would work together again. In 2011 I was doing an “MTO Plays the Early Blues” concert at a summer series in NYC. The promoter, Jay Weisman, asked if I’d like to have Henry Butler play, and I said of course, but where is he? It turned out he had an apartment in Brooklyn, post Katrina. When the concert was over Henry called me and said we should do a show with MTO playing all of his music – that was the birth of Butler Bernstein and the Hot 9 (there were 10 people in the band). As far as my working relationship, he totally trusted my bandleading instincts and arranging, and I was always awed and inspired by the music flowing out of him.

TC: You bring up a salient point. Around the time of the Kansas City soundtrack, there seemed to be a very healthy major label interest in jazz that benefitted musicians of all stripes, even those somewhat on the fringe (James Carter, Don Byron, David Murray, etc.), which to me, evoked the pre-Young Lions era, when major labels signed post-loft jazz artists like Anthony Braxton, Arthur Blythe, and Henry Threadgill.

Much has changed since then. I’m curious what your thoughts are on that phenomenon? How have you adapted to the changing fortunes of the recording business? And what do you foresee for the future?

SB: Well, the beautiful thing is that I have been DIY since the beginning. I think the budget of the first Spanish Fly record (which was on Knitting Factory Records) was 3K, and Hal Willner produced it! I personally have never really had a record contract where I was signed and had a budget. I’ve had a few independent contracts, and records funded by public and private grants. That is the way everything is now, so it’s just the way I’ve always been able to create new things. And that’s what it’s about, creating new things.

items.body:
Bass on Top

a column by
Andrey Henkin

Arjen Gorter, with and without Willem Breuker




The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items.body: Soft Confidence bathes in the fading light of dusk. The tanned, glowing synths emerge from a rented beach house while the sunset-gazing keys stand around, clustered together like the best of friends, a cold drink in one hand and a cell phone – locked, loaded, and ready to take an insane amount of group photos – in the other. Melodies glimmer. The lo-fi thrums are as distant as thunder in another country. They intermittently strobe, winking in and out of the music’s focus, like French lights glimpsed from an English harbour. The music looks out at the listener through a silky veil. Australian composer and producer Richard Pike, aka Deep Learning, has populated his new album with both a joyous spirit and a dying light. Sparkling like a can of Sprite, these melodies emerge and fizzle out. Garbled electronics enter and then fade, emanating from an old radio with tuning problems. Emotions are rubbed into the music’s skin like sunscreen; they melt into its soft curves. Synths are so often cold, sterile, and sharp enough to pinprick the song’s skin, but these synths are the opposite of that, dripping instead with a soft, lubricating shower gel, the bubbles in its bubble-bath rising and dipping like foamy notes on a steamy stave, leaving the listener both cleansed and purified. Releasing on his own label Salmon Universe, Soft Confidence is music of subtle ambient brushes and wholehearted feels, bringing to mind a neon-lit world drunk on cocktails of fluorescent after-dark lighting and innocent romance, of shared sweet kisses under the artificial glow of a streetlight, the authentic emotion illuminated by simulated light and digital synth. It started off as a series of sketches for an installation project by London’s United Visual Artistsat the Tokyo National Museum, but the music has now morphed into a fully-grown, mature album of soft-blowing, romanticized synths, bubble-wrapped in a light hiss and attired in the loose, baggy jeans of beatless ambient. No sharp edges exist. Instead, soft, lipstick-smeared melodies and pulsating keys are the order of the day (or evening), with some sweet Asian flavours mixed into the recipe – the recurring staccato phrases of ‘Firefly’ have something inherently Japanese about them, as does the aptly-named ‘Tokyo Slowdown’, which eschews the fast-paced onslaught of life in the West – not that Tokyo is any slower – for a slice of hillside peace. Although Tokyo never seems to sleep, the music immediately brings about a sense of stillness and stasis without sleepwalking into lethargy; a vital outlet for rush-hour living, and a moment of necessary balancing; the inbuilt need for calm and rest will always wrestle with the twelve-hour-long stresses of another day, but for now, let’s enjoy this moment. “The music was a respite from all the other music I was making at the time. It fulfilled me to make these small but expansive vignettes – of inner and outer life. I enjoyed creating quickly, finding a perfect moment before it became over-produced – a sense of balance that I was also looking for in my life. Ambient music is something I’ve always wanted to make. And I believe in our current times, this kind of spiritual music is more relevant than ever.” www.salmonuniverse.com
items._cn_summary: 澳大利亚制作人Richard Pike以Deep Learning名义发行的这张专辑，起初是为伦敦视觉艺术家团体在东京国立博物馆的装置项目所作的草稿，后经发展形成完整的氛围电子作品。整体音乐呈现出暮色般的柔和光泽，合成器音色温暖低饱和，没有尖锐棱角，以无拍的环境音为主调。评论以细腻的意象描绘其声音质感——晚霞光线、海边出租屋、怀旧闪烁的电子噪声、如泡泡浴般的润滑音色。专辑融入亚洲元素，部分曲目带有明显的日本色彩，在都市快节奏与静谧冥想之间寻找平衡。评论将这张作品定位为快节奏生活中的喘息时刻，以精巧的电子小品呈现内外生活的片段。
